framework.principle: Campbell proposes that myths from divergent traditions can be compared for recurring structures, while acknowledging that particular traditions differ.
The book uses psychoanalysis as one interpretive aid for mythic imagery, not as a conclusively proven key to every tradition.
An often-repeated heroic design moves from ordinary life through separation and ordeal toward a return with something that matters beyond the protagonist.
Campbell makes a composite from many myths; a particular narrative need not enact each stage as a discrete event.
Campbell relates the image-life of private dreams to culturally shared stories without claiming their contexts are identical.
Ritual trials can mark a change of social and psychic status; hero narratives enlarge this passage pattern into cosmic terms.
The hero is transformed inwardly, but the return concerns relationships and the larger world.
Engulfment, darkness and dismemberment dramatize dissolution of an established identity and the possibility of another mode of life.
The sought gift may be food, fire, health, sovereignty, instruction or insight, depending on the story.
Boundaries can protect as well as imprison; confronting the unknown carries risk and opportunity.
Goddess, temptress and father motifs are drawn from Campbell’s mid-twentieth-century psychoanalytic language and should not be imposed as fixed gender roles.
The creation and dissolution of the universe operate as a larger counterpart to the hero’s passage.
Accounts of the void, generation and separation represent differentiation out of an undivided source.
The hero may figure as novice, warrior, culture-bringer, ruler, redeemer or contemplative, with different ethical implications.
The tyrant or monster-hoarder dramatizes power held for private gain rather than shared communal flourishing.
Campbell’s epilogue acknowledges that myths can be approached through multiple interpretive systems and resists final closure.
The book questions how inherited mythic forms can orient persons when the contemporary world has outgrown many traditional communal frameworks.

chapters.title: Prologue: The Monomyth
chapters.overview: Introduces the comparative claim that narrative, initiation and dream imagery repeatedly portray a departure from the ordinary, contact with transforming powers and a consequential return.
ideas: Myths and dreams can be compared without reducing each to the other.
The heroic pattern relates to separation, ordeal and reintegration.
The world navel images a life-giving axis or source within a mythic cosmos.

chapters.title: Chapter I: Departure
chapters.part: Part I: The Adventure of the Hero
chapters.overview: Develops the beginnings of mythic adventure: summons, hesitation, help, a boundary crossing and the symbolic death of an old identity.
ideas: Unplanned incidents, messengers and loss can summon change.
The refusal and the supernatural helper show contrasting responses to the summons.
Threshold guardians and devouring places give form to the fear of leaving a known world.

chapters.title: Chapter II: Initiation
chapters.part: Part I: The Adventure of the Hero
chapters.overview: Examines the sequence of tests and revelations after the threshold, including encounters with maternal and paternal powers and a transformative acquisition.
ideas: Repeated challenges can dismantle familiar defenses and expand perspective.
A mythic goddess, father or tempter is a role in a comparative reading, not a fixed meaning of an actual person.
The ultimate boon can be material, restorative, social or spiritual.

chapters.title: Chapter III: Return
chapters.part: Part I: The Adventure of the Hero
chapters.overview: Explains the difficulty of bringing extraordinary insight or power back into ordinary relations and of acting from a transformed viewpoint.
ideas: The hero may wish not to return.
Flight, rescue and reentry dramatize the need to move between unlike modes of experience.
A successful adventure becomes relevant to others only when its benefit can circulate socially.

chapters.title: Chapter IV: The Keys
chapters.part: Part I: The Adventure of the Hero
chapters.overview: Offers a compact synthesis of the comparative heroic sequence and its relationship to rebirth and cosmic imagery.
ideas: The pattern is a compositional guide rather than a timetable required of every narrative.
Encountering the threshold and returning are both types of transformation.

chapters.title: Chapter I: Emanations
chapters.overview: Traces mythic accounts of how undifferentiated being or an unformed source becomes a populated world of space, time and living differentiation.
ideas: Cosmogonies narrate a transition from unmanifest potential to plurality.
Myths of cyclic creation locate worlds within repeated emergence and withdrawal.
Images such as the void, cosmic egg and splitting of an original unity shape this account.

chapters.title: Chapter II: The Virgin Birth
chapters.overview: Studies world-mother and exceptional-birth traditions as images of generative possibility within the cosmic cycle.
ideas: The generative mother is read symbolically as a medium of manifestation.
Stories of unusual births connect historical or heroic destinies with cosmic origin.

chapters.title: Chapter III: Transformations of the Hero
chapters.overview: Follows successive hero roles from semi-divine beings into increasingly human history, including child, warrior, lover, ruler, redeemer and saint.
ideas: The hero takes historically different forms as myth passes toward legend.
Heroic conquest can be criticized when it repeats tyranny.
Great heroes may bring laws, social renewal or spiritual teachings rather than victory in battle.

chapters.title: Chapter IV: Dissolutions
chapters.overview: Considers mythic endings of personal existence and of cosmic worlds as complementary scales of dissolution.
ideas: Individual death is presented as a transformation relative to enduring cosmic order.
Some apocalyptic images complete a cycle that can begin again.

chapters.title: Epilogue: Myth and Society
chapters.overview: Returns to the purposes of myth, the plurality of interpretive approaches and the modern challenge of finding orienting imagery amid altered social conditions.
ideas: No single explanatory system exhausts myth.
Myth connects inner development, group life and the unsayable.
The contemporary person must face conditions not adequately described by an inherited social map.

eliade.title: Images and Symbols: Studies in Religious Symbolism
eliade.author: Mircea Eliade
eliade.label: Mircea Eliade, Images and Symbols: Studies in Religious Symbolism, tr. Philip Mairet (1952)

bib.title: Images and Symbols: Studies in Religious Symbolism
bib.author: Mircea Eliade

framework.principle: For Eliade, symbolic thought is a meaningful mode of knowing; images are not merely decorations on propositions.
A significant image can hold multiple related or opposed possibilities, and exclusive reduction to one meaning impoverishes it.
Symbols and mythical patterns can persist in ostensibly secular desires, narratives, nostalgia and ordinary imagination.
Both tracing how a symbol traveled or changed and analyzing the structural relations within its imagery are needed.
Archaic sacred geography frequently gives primacy to a privileged space imagined as linking levels of the cosmos.
Reenacting a beginning can convert a local act of founding or celebration into renewed cosmic creation.
Mythic narration and ritual may change the experienced relation between ordinary duration and exemplary, sacred time.
Myths of overwhelming cosmic cycles may motivate the pursuit of liberation beyond unstable conditioned existence.
Binding techniques can protect as well as constrain; a recurrent shape does not have a stable value outside its context.
Shells, pearls, and lunar patterns are analyzed as an interrelated cluster around generativity, death, and restoration.
Older symbolic patterns may persist through changed ritual uses, new narratives or new cultural valuations.
Christian meanings of cross, baptism and sacred events must not be flattened into comparative parallels alone.
Symbolic significance may add to an object’s historical and immediate value without invalidating its everyday function.
The comparative method must not erase contextual variations or assume that formal similarities prove an identical origin.

chapters.title: Symbolism of the “Centre”
chapters.overview: Sacred space is ordered around a privileged location imagined as the place where cosmic levels communicate. Mountains, trees, pillars, temples, houses, ritual ascents and mandalas offer different cultural realizations of that pattern.
ideas: The lived world is ritually differentiated from its surrounding chaos.
A center can be established anew in multiple sanctuaries; sacred centrality need not indicate one geographic coordinate.
Ascent and inward movement figure access to otherwise separated cosmic levels.
Building sacred space can repeat the original creation of the cosmos.

chapters.title: Indian Symbolisms of Time and Eternity
chapters.overview: Mythic narratives about vast cycles of cosmic creation and destruction disclose the precariousness of ordinary historical duration. Eliade examines Indian images and disciplines that contrast time-bound existence with liberation or an unchanging present.
ideas: Recounting primordial events can make sacred time present again.
Immense cycles and repeated world-destructions can provoke the desire for liberation.
Images such as a motionless sun, a broken egg and the Buddha’s seven steps dramatize transcendence of normal space and time.
Yoga and regulated breath can be interpreted as re-patterning human rhythms in relation to cosmic rhythms.

chapters.title: The “God Who Binds” and the Symbolism of Knots
chapters.overview: Ropes, snares, knots, and releases appear across myths and rituals as images of supernatural sovereignty, capture, destiny, illness, protection, subjection, and release. Eliade argues that they belong to related but distinct religious and magical systems.
ideas: Varuna represents a form of magical sovereignty associated with binding and punishment.
Indra’s overcoming of an obstructing adversary offers a contrasting image of release.
The same material knot may protect, constrain or endanger depending on the rite.
Comparative similarity is not proof of common origin or identical cultural function.

chapters.title: Observations on the Symbolism of Shells
chapters.overview: Eliade examines shells, oysters, pearls, and spirals in relation to lunar and aquatic rhythms, feminine generativity, amulets, marriage, initiation, burial, folk medicine and religious images of spiritual treasure.
ideas: The lunar–aquatic–fertility constellation can organize several otherwise separate uses of shells.
Shells and pearls may accompany both reproductive rites and the hoped-for regeneration of the dead.
A valued ornament may outlive, obscure or transform an earlier ritual significance.
The pearl may acquire an explicitly spiritual meaning in Gnostic and Christian contexts.

chapters.title: Symbolism and History
chapters.overview: Aquatic symbolism and the Christian rites of baptism exemplify how inherited images can take on distinctive historical and theological meaning. The conclusion defends the need to interpret both the structure of symbolism and its local history.
ideas: Water can abolish forms and therefore represent both dissolution and renewed birth.
Christian baptism reinterprets older water motifs through narratives of Christ and the Flood.
The cross is considered alongside the pre-Christian world tree and cosmic axis without being reduced to them.
Cultural transformations preserve, alter and contest the meanings of inherited imagery.
Symbolic reading adds a possible level of meaning without negating material or historical reality.

jung.title: Man and His Symbols
jung.author: Carl G. Jung (ed.)
jung.label: Carl G. Jung (ed.), Man and His Symbols (1964)

framework.principle: Jung explicitly distinguishes reference by convention from symbolic expression that exceeds known, immediate meaning.
Dream images require the dreamer’s associations and living situation; the book rejects rule-of-thumb meanings.
Symbols in dreams are described as arising without deliberate invention.
Psychic life includes parts not under conscious control; dreams can make some of their effects visible.
An image can question or balance a conscious attitude rather than simply repeat it.
Archetypal recurrence concerns proposed psychic dispositions; particular images remain historically and personally shaped.
A story or rite may dramatize recognizable patterns of maturing, loss, or psychic transformation.
The initiate often must yield or surrender, whereas the hero narrative emphasizes overcoming an external opponent.
The psyche’s movement toward integration is shown through changing life situations and recurring dream motifs.
A disowned side of character can carry useful vitality as well as socially objectionable impulses.
Anima and animus are presented in a binary gender schema characteristic of Jungian psychology at the time.
The Self is a hypothesized organizing totality, distinct from the conscious ego.
Natural objects, sacred geometry, and modern art can give form to psychological themes without one-to-one translation.
Jacobi’s one-person analysis illustrates a method rather than validating universal interpretations of mountains or lakes.
The final essay asks how non-conscious thought contributes to insight and cautiously juxtaposes psychology and science.

chapters.title: Approaching the Unconscious
chapters.author: Carl G. Jung
chapters.overview: Jung explains how a symbol differs from a sign, why dreams disclose unconscious aspects of mental life, and why interpretation must take the individual dreamer and psychological situation seriously.
ideas: A symbol suggests meanings that exceed a conventional sign or a fully articulated concept.
Dream images are treated as spontaneous communications of the unconscious, not predetermined codewords.
Personal experience, associations, temperament, conscious attitude, and the entire dream context affect interpretation.
Archetypal patterns are linked to inherited psychic dispositions, whereas particular images take historically and personally specific forms.
Modern rational habits may distance conscious thought from the emotional potency of inherited symbolic forms.

chapters.title: Ancient Myths and Modern Man
chapters.author: Joseph L. Henderson
chapters.overview: Henderson connects mythic hero figures, rites of passage, encounters with monsters, and religious narratives with psychological maturation and changing life stages.
ideas: The hero journey frequently dramatizes the growth of the ego and the need to gain independence.
The hero may require supernatural helpers and must eventually recognize vulnerability rather than remain permanently triumphant.
Initiations repeatedly stage separation, ordeal, symbolic death, and return or rebirth.
Mythic death and resurrection can figure a change in attitude rather than a literal event.
Birds, flight, and related modern technologies can symbolize liberation from a restrictive condition.

chapters.title: The Process of Individuation
chapters.author: M.-L. von Franz
chapters.overview: Von Franz presents individuation as a gradual relationship between conscious life and a deeper organizing center of the psyche, using dreams and fairy tales to explore shadow, anima, animus, and images of psychic totality.
ideas: A series of dreams may reveal a developing pattern not visible in a single image.
Individuation is an open-ended process of integration, not conformity to a prefabricated ideal.
A shadow figure may represent disowned impulses and also neglected capacities.
The anima and animus are described through the book’s historically gendered Jungian framework.
Symbols of the Self can include geometric wholes, guides, precious stones, and images of a centered order.
No one can be given a universal script for how inner development ought to unfold.

chapters.title: Symbolism in the Visual Arts
chapters.author: Aniela Jaffé
chapters.overview: Jaffé surveys the sacred and psychological resonances of stones, animals, circles, mandalas, and religious art, then considers the changing symbolic forms of modern painting and abstraction.
ideas: Natural objects can become symbolic when people invest them with sacred or psychic significance.
The circular form recurs in sacred buildings, cosmograms, art, and images of inner wholeness.
Modern artists can give visual form to the irrational and the unconscious without depicting literal dream scenes.
Abstract forms may concentrate psychological meaning even when their subject is not conventionally recognizable.
Changing styles alter the presentation of enduring symbolic problems such as alienation and the relation of opposites.

chapters.title: Symbols in an Individual Analysis
chapters.author: Jolande Jacobi
chapters.overview: Jacobi follows the dream series of a young man, Henry, showing how image meanings emerge from his circumstances, associations, and changes during an analysis rather than from universal assignments.
ideas: The opening mountain-pass dream suggests a transition that the dreamer is not yet prepared to complete.
Figures such as an old woman, monsters, and an inner feminine presence shift in meaning as the dreams evolve.
The lake and submerged locomotives are interpreted in this case as images of inaccessible energy later brought to awareness.
The story is an illustration of one analysis and cannot serve as a reusable diagnostic dream key.
Later dreams are interpreted in the light of earlier ones and of the dreamer’s current life.

chapters.title: Conclusion: Science and the Unconscious
chapters.author: M.-L. von Franz
chapters.overview: Von Franz offers a concluding reflection on unconscious patterning, meaning, scientific creativity, and the limits of strictly causal explanations of psychic life.
ideas: Scientific problems may ripen in unconscious thought and emerge as sudden reorganizations of ideas.
Attention to meaning and pattern complements, rather than straightforwardly replaces, causal explanation.
The chapter draws analogies with developments in physics; those analogies are historical arguments, not experimental proof of Jungian theory.

turner.title: The Forest of Symbols: Aspects of Ndembu Ritual
turner.author: Victor Turner
turner.label: Victor Turner, The Forest of Symbols: Aspects of Ndembu Ritual (1967)

bib.author: Victor Turner
bib.subject: Ethnographic studies of ritual symbolism among the Ndembu of northwestern Zambia
bib.pdf_filename: The Forest of Symbols Aspects of Ndembu Ritual (Victor Turner) (z-library.sk, 1lib.sk, z-lib.sk)(1).pdf

framework.principle: Turner treats symbols as forces within concrete social performances; their role cannot be recovered by merely listing verbal definitions.
Participant exegesis and an analyst’s reading are distinct sources of evidence; specialist and lay explanations can also differ.
A dominant symbol anchors a rite and condenses values considered ends in themselves.
An instrumental symbol takes much of its significance from a specific ritual sequence and its relation to that rite’s central aims.
Important ritual symbols commonly point to several referents at once, through linked images, relations and actions.
A compact symbol or gesture can bring together bodily experiences, social duties and spiritual or emotional concerns.
Turner distinguishes the pole tied to social norms and ideals from the pole drawing upon bodily processes, sensations and affect.
Exegetical meaning is what those involved say a symbol signifies; it must be recorded without mistaking any one speaker for the whole group.
Operational meaning emerges from the actual handling of symbols, participant roles, reactions, and who is absent or excluded.
A symbol’s positional meaning changes with the other objects and actions alongside it in a particular configuration.
White, red, and black form an interacting system that cannot be reduced to universal white-good/red-male/black-evil equations.
Ritual can express common values while also making latent disputes over gender, descent, office and status visible.
Turner distinguishes changes of status such as initiation or death from rites addressed to afflictions attributed to ancestral shades.
Persons in the interval between social statuses may be represented as indeterminate, stripped of previous rank, or compared with death and new birth.
Unexpected combinations in liminal teaching make familiar categories conspicuous by violating normal classifications.
Muchona’s explanations and disagreements with others demonstrate why symbolism requires particular voices and settings.
A rigid classification of occult accusation is less informative than careful examination of lived dynamics and local claims.
Reports of disease causation or cures document Ndembu beliefs and rituals; they are not medical proof of supernatural cause or treatment efficacy.

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.overview: Situates the Ndembu ritual system in the social tensions of matrilineal descent and virilocal residence, and distinguishes life-crisis rites from affliction cults.
ideas: Village mobility and kinship create tensions between the allegiances of fathers, sons, and matrilineal relatives.
Rites of passage alter not only individual statuses but also relations among kin and neighbors.
Rituals of affliction respond to misfortune attributed within Ndembu belief to shades of deceased relatives.

chapters.title: Symbols in Ndembu Ritual
chapters.overview: Introduces the milk tree as a leading example for studying symbols in action and defines dominant and instrumental symbols, condensed and polarized meanings.
ideas: Observe ritual performance and relationships instead of treating symbols as static labels.
A dominant image can express physiological experience and communal values simultaneously.
Ritual symbols do more than communicate: they organize interaction and mobilize groups.

chapters.title: Ritual Symbolism, Morality, and Social Structure among the Ndembu
chapters.overview: Explains the multi-vocal character of ritual symbols and the three fields of evidence used to investigate them.
ideas: Exegetical meaning comes from participants’ accounts.
Operational meaning is found by watching actions, emotions, roles, and exclusions.
Positional meaning depends on the symbol’s relations to other symbols in a particular ritual.

chapters.title: Color Classification in Ndembu Ritual
chapters.overview: Examines the contextual white/red/black triad and critiques simplistic mappings of colors onto sex or moral oppositions.
ideas: White connotes purity, life, health, unity and other qualities; red involves blood, strength, childbirth and danger.
Black commonly marks loss, disease, darkness and death, but its use is situated and is not a stand-alone universal code.
A color can signify different or even opposed things in distinct combinations and performances.

chapters.title: Betwixt and Between: The Liminal Period in Rites de Passage
chapters.overview: Investigates the ambiguous, neither-here-nor-there condition of persons passing between defined statuses.
ideas: Separation, margin/transition and incorporation form an important comparative pattern for passage rites.
Seclusion and instruction rearrange normal distinctions, often through death/birth imagery, disguises and paradoxes.
Sacred objects and deliberately surprising combinations can prompt reflection on a culture’s categories.

chapters.title: Witchcraft and Sorcery: Taxonomy versus Dynamics
chapters.overview: Critiques rigid comparative classifications of witchcraft and sorcery divorced from actual accusations, social situations and processes.
ideas: Analysts should not substitute a crisp classificatory opposition for local historical practice.
Accusations and suspicions are embedded in social relationships and conflicts.

chapters.title: Muchona the Hornet, Interpreter of Religion
chapters.overview: Portrays a knowledgeable Ndembu ritual interpreter whose explanations lead Turner to take local specialists’ theory seriously.
ideas: Indigenous experts formulate elaborate and sometimes competing symbolic interpretations.
Ethnographic understanding grows through argument, translation, context and attention to who is speaking.

chapters.title: Mukanda: The Rite of Circumcision
chapters.overview: Extended field account of the Ndembu boys’ collective initiation, including the movement through ritual spaces, seclusion, instruction, masquerade, and political maneuvering.
ideas: A novice moves symbolically from childhood toward publicly recognized masculinity.
Trees, medicines, fire, gateways, masks and the lodge acquire significance through ordered ritual action.
Kinship, sponsorship and village politics shape the enacted ceremony rather than floating outside it.

chapters.title: Themes in the Symbolism of Ndembu Hunting Ritual
chapters.overview: Analyzes hunting initiation and shrines, especially how the forked branch concentrates both benefits and tensions surrounding skilled hunters.
ideas: Hunting success, ancestral patronage, food-sharing and rivalry are bound together in the shrine.
A hunter’s gains are tied to obligations toward kin and community.
The same symbolic object can unite fertility-like images of abundance and potentially bitter social conflict.

chapters.title: Lunda Medicine and the Treatment of Disease
chapters.overview: Studies how therapeutic preparations and procedures use classification, analogies and social relationships in local healing practices.
ideas: Treatments are analyzed as culturally coherent ritual practice, not evidence of biomedical efficacy.
Colors, plants, washing, cooling, expulsion and movement help render troubles symbolically manageable.
Medicine and ritual are interconnected with ideas about social breach and ancestor relations.

chapters.title: A Ndembu Doctor in Practice
chapters.overview: Close-grained account of an Ihamba healing sequence in which bodily treatment, confession, social relations and the hunter shade are brought into one public ritual.
ideas: A putative tooth-like afflicting entity is made actionable through ritual intervention.
Publicly expressed grievances can be part of the rite’s social working.
The observer should distinguish what participants say happened from what can be independently established.

cirlot.title: A Dictionary of Symbols
cirlot.author: J. E. Cirlot
cirlot.label: J. E. Cirlot, A Dictionary of Symbols, tr. Jack Sage (1971)

framework.principle: Cirlot treats symbolic meaning as a layer of interpretation rather than an exhaustive account of an object or historical event.
Symbols can sustain multiple interacting meanings, while simple one-to-one translations risk turning them into flattened allegory.
A symbolic interpretation need not deny that a narrative, object, or event also has practical and historical standing.
Relationships of form, function, action, and position allow unlike things to enter shared symbolic patterns.
The book considers diffusion, recurring cultural motifs, and possible shared psychic structures as different explanations of similarity.
Dream symbols can share structures with mythic symbols, but dreams also contain ordinary memories and physiological material.
Cirlot presents alchemical work as materially pursued and symbolically open to readings of psychic and spiritual change.
Following Jung, Cirlot discusses recurring image patterns as powerful organizers of psychic experience without simply equating every image with an archetype.
One motif can function simultaneously at natural, psychological, cultural, and spiritual levels rather than having a single invariant gloss.
An object's form, action, position, relation to neighbors, and location inside a composition can all alter its symbolic role.
Symbols in dreams, art, rites, and stories often operate as structured clusters rather than independent dictionary tokens.
The work documents interpretations associated with symbolic traditions and selected thinkers; it should not be used to present a universal psychological law as established fact.

tresidder.title: The Complete Dictionary of Symbols
tresidder.author: Jack Tresidder (ed.)
tresidder.label: Jack Tresidder (ed.), The Complete Dictionary of Symbols (2004)

framework.principle: Images of ordinary creatures or objects can acquire culturally transmitted meanings well beyond their practical uses.
Similar visible forms can receive significantly different valuations in different cultural settings; the dragon is a central example.
Coincidences between cultures are worth noting without treating all traditions as interchangeable.
Art, ritual and ornament use recognizable attributes to convey theological, ethical and social messages.

framework.principle: An image is treated as an invitation to fresh meaning, not a code with one permanent decoded answer.
Essays attend to the material properties, form, movement, and behavior of their subject before exploring symbolic associations.
The book is a curated collaboration; its essays were deliberately allowed distinct voices rather than rewritten as one uniform doctrine.
Artwork and essay were conceived together, with the image serving as the prompt for reflection rather than an illustration added afterwards.
Symbols remain multivalent and can connect seemingly incompatible emotional or intellectual associations.
Archetypal forms are compared across art, ritual, myth, dreams, fantasies, and cultural traditions, while their uses differ.
A cultural motif or psychological analogy should not be treated as a deterministic interpretation of a particular person or dream.
Associations projected onto things may offer insight or obscure the actual specificity of an object.
Word origins, opposing meanings, religious practices, and cultural differences provide multiple routes into a symbol.
Cosmological symbols repeatedly connect hidden origins with gestation, illumination, differentiation, and return.
Plants and animals link observed bodily characteristics with questions of survival, fertility, transformation, and instinct.
Human-made objects and dwellings can serve as analogies for inner life, social belonging, orientation, and boundaries.
Roads, water crossings, stairs, and spirals give shape to initiation, choice, and change of state.
Death-related forms are not uniformly negative: some myths pair dissolution and burial with renewed or altered life.
Concrete mythological examples are culturally situated; similarities across societies do not demonstrate identical meanings.

Birds are vertebrate animals constituting the class Aves, characterised by feathers, toothless beaked jaws, the laying of hard-shelled eggs, a high metabolic rate, a four-chambered heart, and a strong yet lightweight skeleton.

Black is a color that results from the absence or complete absorption of visible light. It is an achromatic color, without chroma, like white and grey. It is often used symbolically or figuratively to represent darkness.

The Black Stone (Arabic: الحجر الأسود, romanized: al-Ḥajar al-Aswad) is a rock set into the eastern corner of the Kaaba, the ancient building in the center of the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca, Saudi Arabia.
UFOs reported as having a triangular shape and dark color, typically observed at night, described as large, silent, hovering, moving slowly, and displaying pulsating, colored lights.

A sacred object, imbued with magic, in Grail ceremonies. Drops of blood issue from its point. When the Grail is Christianized, this weapon transforms into the Holy Lance, the spear that pierced the side of Jesus by the hand of a Roman…
In religion, a blessing (also used to refer to the bestowing of one) is the impartation grace, holiness, spiritual redemption, or divine will upon a person, object, or endeavor.

The blood shed by Jesus Christ on the Cross.

Blue is one of the three primary colours in the RGB (additive) colour model, as well as in the RYB colour model (traditional colour theory). It lies between violet and cyan on the spectrum of visible light.

A symbol of the sun, since the flowers are closed at night and open again in the morning. The origin of the world was taught to have been when the sun god Ra emerged from a lotus flower growing in "primordial waters".

Heime (German), Háma (Old English: Hāma), or Heimir (Old Norse) was a Germanic figure in Germanic heroic legend who often appears together with his friend Witige. He is mentioned in the Anglo-Saxon poems Beowulf and Widsith.
A boat is a watercraft of a large range of types and sizes, but generally smaller than a ship, which is distinguished by its larger size or capacity, its shape, or its ability to carry boats.
Henry’s boat, barrier, and forbidden view of the water are read as images of his fear of confronting deeper psychic material.
Which carries souls of the newly deceased across the rivers Styx and Acheron that divided the world of the living from the world of the dead.

The Bodhi tree (Sanskrit and Pāli: Bodhi meaning "awakening" or "enlightenment") is the specific Bo tree (from the Sinhala bo, derived from bodhi)—a sacred fig (Ficus religiosa)—located within the Buddhist Mahabodhi Temple, a UNESCO World…
In Buddhism, a bodhisattva is a person who has attained, or is striving towards, bodhi (meaning ‘awakening', 'enlightenment') or Buddhahood.

A bone is a rigid organ that constitutes part of the skeleton in most vertebrate animals. Bones protect the organs of the body, produce red and white blood cells, store minerals, help regulate acid-base homeostasis, provide structure and…

A book is a written work of substantial length created by one or more authors. The work is typically printed on many sheets of paper as pages bound together into a bookblock, then glued to the middle of a foldable cover that protects the…
The book in which God records the names of every person who is destined for Heaven or the World to Come.
Book of Thoth is a name given to many ancient Egyptian texts attributed to Thoth, the Egyptian god of writing and knowledge.
An acquired benefit that remedies some lack or disorder, ranging from useful things to an illuminating teaching.
The bow and arrow is a ranged weapon system consisting of an elastic launching device (bow) and long-shafted projectiles (arrows).
A female Christian knight who wields a magical lance that unhorses anyone it touches.
A magical golden harp given to Bragi by the dwarfs when he was born.
It is said in the epic Mahabharata that the weapon manifests with the all five heads of Lord Brahma as its tip. Brahma earlier lost his fifth head when he fought with Lord Shiva.
It is thought that the Brahmashirsha Astra is the evolution of the Brahmastra, and 4 times stronger than Brahmastra. The weapon manifests with the four heads of Lord Brahma as its tip.

The Brahmastra (Sanskrit: ब्रह्मास्त्र, romanized: Brahmāstra, lit. 'Astra of Brahma') is the supreme Hindu celestial weapon (astra) created and owned by the god Brahma along with its more powerful variant, the Brahmashirastra.
The sword of Hereward the Wake.
An alleged torture and execution device invented by Perillos of Athens, who offered it to Phalaris, the tyrant of Akragas, Sicily, as a new means of executing criminals.
A legendary automaton reputed to be able to answer any question.
Bread is a baked food product made from water, flour, and often yeast. It is a staple food across the world, particularly in Europe and the Middle East.
Breathing (respiring or ventilating) is the rhythmic process of inhaling air into the lungs providing oxygen, and exhaling the air removing carbon dioxide, in the gas exchange process.
In countless stories from different cultures featured gods breathing life into object that brought them to life.

A bridge is a structure designed to span an obstacle, such as a river or railway, allowing vehicles, pedestrians, and other loads to pass across. Most bridges consist of a flat deck, supported by beams, arches, or cables.
Said to be made from the nails used during the crucifixion of Christ.
Breaking out of an egg dramatizes spiritual birth beyond the first biological birth and the limits enclosing ordinary life.
In Norse mythology, Brísingamen (or Brísinga men) is the torc or necklace of the goddess Freyja, of which little else is known for certain.

Buddha's footprints (Sanskrit: Buddhapada)( Tibetan: སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞབས་རྗེས། ) is an important Buddhist symbol which is commonly depicted as icons shaped like an imprint of Gautama Buddha's foot or both feet.
Images of the Buddha communicate awakened insight through posture, gesture and attributes rather than a single fixed emblem.

Cattle are prominent in some religions and mythologies. As such, numerous peoples throughout the world have at one point in time honored bulls as sacred. In the Sumerian religion, Marduk is the "bull of Utu".
Burial, also known as interment or inhumation, is a method of final disposition whereby a dead body is placed into the ground or in a structure such as a mausoleum, sometimes with objects.
A haunted oak chair that was cursed by the murderer Thomas Busby before his execution by hanging in North Yorkshire, United Kingdom.

Butterflies are winged insects from the lepidopteran superfamily Papilionoidea, characterised by large, often brightly coloured wings that often fold together when at rest, and a conspicuous, fluttering flight.
The movement from larva to winged creature makes metamorphosis visible and suggests fragile freedom and psychic change.
Drawn by metallic, fire-breathing horses.
The winged staff of Hermes (Roman Mercury), with two snakes twined around it: originally the wand of a herald, which made its bearer untouchable on a diplomatic errand.
A fortress in Arfon in northern Gwynedd referred to in the Four Branches of the Mabinogi, the Tale of Math fab Mathonwy.
A legendary otherworld fortress mentioned in Middle Welsh mythological poems in the Book of Taliesin.
Caladbolg ("hard cleft", also spelled Caladcholg, "hard blade") is the sword of Fergus mac Róich from the Ulster Cycle of Irish mythology. Fergus calls his sword by that name in Táin Bó Cúailnge.
Excalibur is the mythical sword of King Arthur that was purported to possess magical powers and be associated with the rightful sovereignty of Britain.
A mythical ghost ship of the Chilote mythology and local folklore of the Chiloé Island, in Chile.
A disruption, message or discovery draws the protagonist away from a settled pattern toward a consequential unknown.
The most valuable part of a Camahueto is their single horn, machis will use the horn for curing many kinds of illnesses.

Cancer (♋︎; Ancient Greek: Καρκίνος, romanized: Karkínos, lit. 'crab', Latin for the "Crab") is the fourth astrological sign in the zodiac, originating from the constellation of Cancer. It spans from 90° to 120° celestial longitude.

A candle is an ignitable wick embedded in wax, or another flammable solid substance such as tallow, that provides light, and in some cases, a fragrance. A candle can also provide heat or a method of keeping time.
Able to expand so it could hold an army, or shrink to fit in the palm of your hand.
It became the South Island of New Zealand.
(Cana's Harp), Canola realised the wind had created the music by blowing through partially rotted sinew still attached to a whale skeleton. She designed the harp based on this.

In classical mythology, the Cap of Invisibility (Ἅϊδος κυνέη (H)aïdos kyneē in Greek, lit. dog-skin of Hades) is a helmet or cap that can turn the wearer invisible, also known as the Cap of Hades or Helm of Hades.

Capricorn (♑︎; Ancient Greek: Αιγόκερως, romanized: Aigókerōs, Latin for "horned goat") is the tenth astrological sign in the zodiac out of twelve total zodiac signs, originating from the constellation of Capricornus, the goat.
The four directions organize a ritual cosmos and may assign distinct colors, deities or powers to each quarter.

Carnwennan ("Little White Hilt") was the dagger of King Arthur in the Welsh Arthurian legends. In Culhwch and Olwen, Arthur names it as one of the few things in the world which he will not give to Culhwch.

A mile-wide cauldron which the Æsir wanted to brew beer in.
The bottomless cauldron of the Dagda, the "good god" of the Irish Tuatha Dé Danann: one of their four great treasures, from which no company ever went away unsatisfied.

Caves and caverns are natural voids under the surface of the Earth and have also been observed in other rocky worlds (e.g., on Mars). Caves often form by the weathering of rock and can extend deep underground.
The Smith of the Branches, sword of Oisín.
The Celtic cross is a form of ringed cross, a Christian cross featuring a nimbus or ring, that emerged in Ireland and Britain in the Early Middle Ages.
A central point can indicate an ordering relation among otherwise dispersed aspects of psychic life.

"reminders" or "memorials" (Sanskrit caitya) are objects and places used by Theravada Buddhists to remember Gautama Buddha.
Chai or Hai (Hebrew: חַי ḥay "living") is a symbol that figures prominently in modern Jewish culture; the Hebrew letters of the word are often used as a visual symbol.

A chain is a serial assembly of connected links typically made of metal, with an overall character similar to that of a rope in that it is flexible and curved in compression, but linear, rigid, and load-bearing in tension.
The chakana or Andean cross (also "stepped cross", "step motif", or "stepped motif") is a stepped cross motif used by the Inca and pre-Incan Andean societies.

An energy point or node in the subtle body. Chakras are believed to be part of the subtle body, not the physical body, and as such, are the meeting points of the subtle (non-physical) energy channels called Nadi.
A chalice (from Latin calix 'cup', taken from the Ancient Greek κύλιξ (kylix) 'cup') is a drinking cup raised on a stem with a foot or base.
In the Hindu epic Ramayana, the Chandrahansa sword is an indestructible sword that Lord Shiva gifts Ravana.

Chandrahasa (Sanskrit: चन्द्रहास, lit. 'laughter of the moon') is a king of the Kuntala kingdom in Hindu mythology. The story of Chandrahasa is described in the Ashvamedhika Parva of the epic Mahabharata.
Legendary sword of Manjusri, according to Swayambhu Purana used to found Kathmandu Valley, forms the centerpiece of flag of Kathmandu.
What lies outside a sanctified domain is sometimes represented as disorder or dissolution, against which the inhabited world is maintained.
The chariot that carried the prophet Elijah to heaven.

A charmstone or coldstone is a stone or mineral artifact of various types associated with various traditional cultures, including those of Scotland and the native cultures of California and the American southwest.

Cobra is the common name of various venomous snakes, most of which belong to the genus Naja. Many cobras are capable of rearing upwards and producing a hood when threatened.

Or cochaillín draíochta is a special hat worn by merrows which enables them to travel between deep water and dry land. If they lose this cap, it is said that they will lose their power to return beneath the water.

White, red and black jointly classify vital and moral aspects of Ndembu experience; meaning depends on the triad and the ritual setting.
Five colored stones crafted by the goddess Nüwa that each represent one of the five Chinese elements, fire, water, earth, metal, and wood.
Color (or colour in Commonwealth English) is the visual perception produced by the activation of the different types of cone cells in the eye caused by light.
The column which Jesus was tied to during the Flagellation of Christ, kept in the Basilica of Saint Praxedes in Rome.

(Berenice's hair), Berenice II of Egypt dedicated her hair to Aphrodite for her husband's safe return from Syria, and placed it in the temple of the goddess at Zephyrium. The hair had been carried to the heavens and placed among the stars.
A comet is an icy, small Solar System body or interstellar object that warms and begins to release gases when passing close to the Sun, a process called outgassing.
The return makes private transformation consequential through instruction, healing, provision or another service to others.
The dream may balance or challenge an overly narrow conscious attitude by giving a voice to a neglected counter-perspective.
A synthetic map assembled from distinct stories; it emphasizes parallels without functioning as a literal account of one legend.
Condensation is the change of the state of matter from the gas phase into the liquid phase, and is the reverse of vaporization. The word most often refers to the water cycle.

A hidden cache of gold lost after the American Civil War. Millions of dollars' worth of gold was lost or unaccounted for after the war and has been the speculation of many historians and treasure hunters.
One of a number of otherworldly wells that are variously depicted as "The Well of Wisdom", "The Well of Knowledge" and the source of some of the rivers of Ireland.
The first of the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse rides on a White Horse is Conquest, and he who sat on it had a bow.
The first of the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse, Conquest, rides a white horse and a crown was given to him.

Consciousness is being aware of something internal to one's self, or of states or objects in one's external environment. It has been the topic of extensive explanations, analyses, and debate among philosophers, scientists, and theologians…
Cooling is removal of heat, usually resulting in a lower temperature and/or phase change. Temperature lowering achieved by any other means may also be called cooling.

The horn of plenty: a goat's or river god's horn overflowing with fruit, grain and flowers, the classical symbol of abundance and good fortune.
Corona Australis is a constellation in the Southern Celestial Hemisphere. Its Latin name means "southern crown", and it is the southern counterpart of Corona Borealis, the northern crown.

Corona Borealis is a small constellation in the Northern Celestial Hemisphere. It is one of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy, and remains one of the 88 modern constellations.

A bag crafted by Manannán mac Lir from the skin of Aoife who had been transformed into a crane at the time of her death. It was later given to Conaire Mór and then eventually to Cumhall mac Trénmhóir and finally Fionn Mac Cumhaill.
The sword of Otuel; Middle English rendition of the sword Corsouse ("Wrathful") of Otinel.

Cortain (also spelled Courtain, Cortana, Curtana, Cortaine or Corte) is the short sword of the legendary Ogier the Dane, a paladin of Charlemagne's court. The name is the accusative case declension of Old French corte, meaning "short".
The Great Triumphant One, sword of Oscar.
Indian accounts of enormous recurring epochs place human events within a scale of repeated universal formation, decline and dissolution.

A prominent sacred mountain may mark the meeting point of heaven and earth, making ascent an approach to the extraordinary.
The world-supporting column is another vertical form by which sacred geography imagines an ordered relation between cosmic levels.
A second large-scale sequence showing the world’s emergence from undifferentiated being, diversification and eventual dissolution.
Cosmology (from Ancient Greek κόσμος (cosmos) 'the universe, the world' and -λογία (logia) 'study of') is the study of the nature of the universe, the cosmos.
A hypothetical planet always on the other side of the Sun from Earth.
Cattle (Bos taurus) are large, domesticated, bovid ungulates widely kept as livestock. They are prominent modern members of the subfamily Bovinae and the most widespread species of the genus Bos.

Cowrie or cowry (pl. cowries) is the common name for a group of small to large sea snails in the family Cypraeidae. Cowrie shells have held cultural, economic, and ornamental significance in various cultures.

Cranes are a type of large bird with long legs and necks in the biological family Gruidae of the order Gruiformes. The family has 15 species placed in four genera which are Antigone, Balearica, Leucogeranus, and Grus.

(Cup), identified with the cup of the god Apollo.

Cronus castrated his father Uranus using an adamant sickle given to him by his mother Gaia.
The cross is a geometrical figure consisting of two intersecting lines or bars, usually perpendicular to each other. The lines usually run vertically and horizontally.

In folklore, crossroads may represent a location "between the worlds" and, as such, a site where supernatural spirits can be contacted and paranormal events can take place.
A dark, resourceful bird evokes omen, uncanny intelligence, transformation, and the boundary between life and death.

A crown is a traditional form of head adornment, or hat, worn by monarchs as a symbol of their power and dignity. A crown is often, by extension, a symbol of the monarch's government or items endorsed by it.

The Crown of Immortality is a literary and religious metaphor traditionally represented in art first as a laurel wreath and later as a symbolic circle of stars (often a crown, tiara, halo or aureola).

Cryptomnesia occurs when a forgotten memory returns without it being recognized as such by the subject, who believes it is something new and original.
A crystal ball is a crystal or glass ball commonly used in fortune-telling. It is generally associated with the performance of clairvoyance and scrying through crystal gazing.
Some individuals believe in the paranormal claim that crystal skulls can produce a variety of miracles.
A Mapuche drum that the Machi's use for healing.
A culture hero is a mythological hero specific to some group (cultural, ethnic, religious, etc.) who changes the world through invention or discovery.
A cup is a small container used to hold liquids for drinking, typically with a flattened hemispherical shape and an open "mouth", and often with a capacity of about 6–16 US fluid ounces (177–473 ml).
The Cup of Jamshid (Persian: جام جم, jām-e Jam) is a cup of divination, which in Persian mythology was long possessed by the rulers of ancient Greater Iran.

Death is the end of an organism's life. It is the irreversible cessation of biological functions that sustain a living organism. Entropy, nature's tendency toward disorder, can contribute to the breakdown of living systems over time.
The fourth of the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse rides on a Pale Horse is Death, he is commonly depict carrying a scythe.

The separation phase in which familiar identity and familiar surroundings cease to be sufficient.

A downward route moves toward buried memory, trial, death, or the fertile interior from which life returns.

The end of individual embodied life is represented as a change in scale or relation to a larger cosmic background.
The djed, also djt (Ancient Egyptian: ḏd 𓊽, Coptic ϫⲱⲧ jōt "pillar", anglicized /dʒɛd/) is one of the more ancient and commonly found symbols in ancient Egyptian religion.
The dog (Canis familiaris or Canis lupus familiaris) is a domesticated descendant of wolves. Also called the domestic dog, it was selectively bred during the Late Pleistocene by hunter-gatherers.

A dolphin is any one of the 40 extant species of aquatic mammal from the cetacean families Delphinidae (the oceanic dolphins), Platanistidae (the Indian river dolphins), Iniidae (the New World river dolphins), Pontoporiidae (the brackish…
A focal symbol recurs across settings and concentrates enduring commitments, frequently organizing the gathering and its emotionally charged actions.
A sacred tree of the Germanic pagans located in what is now the region of Hesse, Germany.
Adinkra symbol of the Akan people. Literal meaning: “The dono drum”.
Adinkra symbol of the Akan people. Literal meaning: “The double dono drums”.
A door is a hinged or otherwise movable barrier that allows ingress (entry) into and egress (exit) from an enclosure. The created opening in the wall is a doorway or portal.
A tiny concentrated point can stand for origin, seed, unity, and the potential of unlimited extension.

Doves, typically domestic pigeons white in plumage, are used in many settings as symbols of peace, freedom, or love. Doves appear in the symbolism of Judaism, Christianity, Islam and paganism, and pacifist groups.

In mainstream Trinitarian Christianity, the Holy Spirit or Holy Ghost (Greek: Ἅγιο Πνεῦμα, Latin: Spiritus Sanctus) is the third Person of the Trinity, which is often enumerated as God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit.
A mythical gemstone taken from the head of a dragon and believed to have magical properties.

A dragon is a mythical creature found in the folklore of cultures throughout the world. It is roughly serpentine in form, and often possesses features drawn from different animals, such as wings and claws.

In the legends of the Phoenician prince Cadmus and in Jason's quest for the Golden Fleece. In each case, the dragons are real and breathe fire. Their teeth, once planted, would grow into fully armed warriors.

A snare drum that Sir Francis Drake took with him when he circumnavigated the world. Shortly before he died he ordered the drum to be taken to Buckland Abbey and vowed that if England was ever in danger and someone was to beat the drum he…

In Norse mythology, Draupnir (Old Norse: [ˈdrɔupnez̠], "the dripper") is a gold ring possessed by the god Odin with the ability to multiply itself: Every ninth night, eight new rings 'drip' from Draupnir, each one of the same size and…
A dream is a succession of images, dynamic scenes and situations, ideas, emotions, and sensations that usually occur involuntarily in the mind during certain stages of sleep.
Changes across Henry’s dreams are used to test how his psychological situation may be shifting rather than assigning an eternal meaning to any one picture.
Repeating or evolving images across several dreams may reveal a more coherent psychic tendency than a single dream considered in isolation.
A dream image matters not only for a possible broad motif but for its exact form and meaning within that dreamer’s situation.

In some Native American and First Nations cultures, a dreamcatcher (Ojibwe: ᐊᓴᐱᑫᔒᓐᐦ, romanized: asabikeshiinh, the inanimate form of the word for 'spider') is a handmade willow hoop, on which is woven a net or web.

Dromi (Hebrew: דרומי) is a Hebrew surname. Notable people with the surname include: Naveh Dromi (1985–2015), Israeli journalist, publicist and TV presenter Pnina Dromi, birth name of Pnina Gary Israeli actress and theatre director Roberto…
The drum is a member of the percussion group of musical instruments. In the Hornbostel–Sachs classification system, it is a membranophone.
A symbol of Druze.
Adinkra symbol of the Akan people. Literal meaning: “The wooden comb”.
The shield of Cú Chulainn.

Durendal, also spelled Durandal, is the sword of Roland, a legendary paladin and partially historical officer of Charlemagne in French epic literature. The sword is famous for its hardness and sharpness.
Adinkra symbol of the Akan people. Literal meaning: “The ram's horns”.

g: Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
entries.o: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain (Welsh: Tri Thlws ar Ddeg Ynys Prydain) are a series of items in late-medieval Welsh tradition. Lists of the items appear in texts dating to the 15th and 16th centuries.

Norse mythology contains references to various named weapons wielded by specific characters. The oldest references sometimes offer nothing except a name for the weapon, but some of them include more detail on the weapon and what makes it…
The eagle is used in heraldry as a charge, as a supporter, and as a crest. Heraldic eagles can be found throughout world history like in the Achaemenid Empire or in the present Republic of Indonesia.
Earth is one of the classical elements, in some systems being one of the four along with air, fire, and water.
(Seax of Ecke), the sword that belonged to the giant Ecke before he was killed by Dietrich von Bern, who then took it for himself.

An eclipse is an astronomical event which occurs when an astronomical object or spacecraft is temporarily obscured, by passing into the shadow of another body or by having another body pass between it and the viewer.
A supposed physical substance that manifests as a result of energy.
Stones struck by lightning, used by Shango.
A sword in the medieval poem Greysteil. Sir Graham obtains the sword 'Egeking' from Eger's aunt, Sir Egram's Lady.

An egg is an organic vessel grown by an animal to carry a possibly fertilized egg cell – a zygote. Within the vessel, an embryo is incubated until it has developed enough to survive on its own, at which point the animal hatches.
Völund is held captive at Nidung's court. To help his brother, Egil shoots birds and collects their feathers, of which Völund makes a pair of wings and flies away.
The center of the conscious standpoint, distinct from the larger totality of the psyche and potentially at odds with unconscious needs.
of Tibetan Buddhism

Consisting of the wish-granting pearl (flaming pearl), the double lozenges, the stone chime, the pair of rhinoceros horns, the double coins, the gold or silver ingot, coral, and the wish-granting scepter.
The cauldron in which Andhrímnir cooks Sæhrímnir.
Earth, water, air, and fire are arranged into a set of contrasting material and spiritual qualities; their interactions help structure symbolic correspondences.

Elephants are the largest living land animals. Three living species are currently recognised: the African bush elephant (Loxodonta africana), the African forest elephant (L. cyclotis), and the Asian elephant (Elephas maximus).

Were arrowheads of flint used in hunting and war by the aborigines of the British Isles and of Europe in general. Elf-Arrows derived their name from the folklore belief that the arrows fell from the sky, and were used by elves to kill…

An elixir is a sweet liquid used for medical purposes, to be taken orally and intended to cure one's illness. When used as a pharmaceutical preparation, an elixir contains at least one active ingredient designed to be taken orally.
A mythical potion that, when drunk from a certain cup at a certain time, supposedly grants the drinker eternal life and/or eternal youth.
Ellida is a genus of moths of the family Notodontidae erected by Augustus Radcliffe Grote in 1876.
The Emerald Tablet, also known as the Smaragdine Table or the Tabula Smaragdina, is a compact and cryptic text traditionally attributed to the legendary Hellenistic figure Hermes Trismegistus.
The unstructured origin becomes a differentiated field in which the action of gods and living beings can take place.
In Hinduism, Jainism and Buddhism, the endless knot or eternal knot is a symbolic knot and one of the Eight Auspicious Symbols.

In Zen art, an ensō (円相; "circular form") is a circle hand-drawn in one or two uninhibited brushstrokes to express the Zen mind, which is associated with enlightenment, emptiness, freedom, and the state of no-mind.
Drawn by two horses.
Adinkra symbol of the Akan people. Literal meaning: “Handcuffs”.
A three-pointed and double-edged spear with two cutting edges of a Saber used by Erlang Shen. It is powerful enough to penetrate and cleave through steel and stone like wool.
A bow wielded by Eros that could cause one to love or hate the person they first saw after being struck.

In philosophy, eternal return (or eternal recurrence) is the concept stating that time repeats itself in an infinite loop, and that exactly the same events will continue to occur in exactly the same way, over and over again, for eternity.

Eurytus became so proud of his archery skills that he challenged Apollo. The god killed Eurytus for his presumption, and Eurytus' bow was passed to Iphitus, who later gave the bow to his friend Odysseus.
A naẓar (from Arabic ‏نَظَر‎ [ˈnaðˤar], meaning 'sight', 'surveillance', 'attention', and other related concepts), or an eye bead, is an eye-shaped amulet believed to protect against the evil eye.
King Arthur's sword: given to him by the Lady of the Lake in some tellings, drawn from a stone in others, and thrown back into the water when he lies dying.
Was said to have powers of its own. Injuries from losses of blood, for example, would not kill the bearer. In some telling, wounds received by one wearing the scabbard did not bleed at all.
Extraordinary circumstances of a figure’s beginning communicate a role set apart by a community’s sacred history.
Meanings offered by indigenous speakers when asked what an observed ritual object or action signifies; speakers may disagree.

An eye is a sensory organ that allows an organism to perceive visual information. It detects light and converts it into electro-chemical impulses in neurons (neurones). It is part of an organism's visual system.
The wedjat, "the sound (whole) one": a stylised human eye with the markings of a falcon's cheek, the eye of the sky god Horus that was torn out by his enemy Set and made whole again.

The Eye of Providence or All-Seeing Eye is a symbol depicting an eye, often enclosed in a triangle and surrounded by rays of light or a halo, intended to represent divine providence watching over mankind.

The Eye of Ra or Eye of Re, usually depicted as sun disk or right wedjat-eye (paired with the Eye of Horus, left wedjat-eye), is an entity in ancient Egyptian mythology that functions as an extension of the sun god Ra's power, equated with…
Sigurd bathed in dragon's blood that conferred him invulnerability. He also drank some of Fafnir's blood and gained the ability to understand the language of the birds.
Which was roasted and consumed by Sigurd, giving him the gift of prophecy.
The bow of Tristan. It was said to never miss its mark.

Tinker Bell is a fictional character from J. M. Barrie's 1904 play Peter Pan and its 1911 novelisation Peter and Wendy. She has appeared in a variety of film and television adaptations of the Peter Pan stories, in particular the 1953…

Falcons () are birds of prey in the genus Falco, which includes about 40 species. Some small species of falcons with long, narrow wings are called hobbies, and some that hover while hunting are called kestrels.
A loss of footing portrays surrender to gravity and may express anxiety, helplessness, or the letting go of control.
The third of the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse rides on a Black Horse is Famine, and he who sat on it had a pair of scales in his hand.
The Farāvahār (Avestan: 𐬟𐬀𐬭𐬎𐬎𐬀𐬵𐬀𐬭𐬀; Persian: فَرْوَهَر), also called the Foruhār (فروهر) or the Fārre Kiyâni (فرّ کیانی), is one of the most prominent symbols of Zoroastrianism.
(Cапоги-скороходы), allows the person wearing them to walk and run at an amazing pace.

A father figure is usually an older man, normally one with power, authority, or strength, with whom one can identify on a deeply psychological level and who generates emotions generally felt towards one's father.

Carrying an hourglass representing time's constant movement. Many believe that Father Time, like the Grim Reaper, is constantly watching humans and has each and every one of their hourglasses slowly decreasing, sand casually slipping…
Feathers are epidermal growths that form a distinctive outer covering, or plumage, on both avian (bird) and some non-avian dinosaurs and other archosaurs.

Her ostrich feather was the measure that determined whether the souls of the departed would reach the fields of Aaru successfully. The hearts of the dead were said to be weighed against her single feather in the Hall of Two Truths.

The Feathered Serpent is a prominent supernatural entity or deity found in many Mesoamerican religions. It is called Quetzalcōātl among the Aztecs; Kukulkan among the Yucatec Maya; and Qʼuqʼumatz and Tohil among the Kʼicheʼ Maya.

The legendary Simurgh gave three of her feathers to Zal, the Persian hero and also father of Rostam, so that whenever he needed the guidance or help of Simurgh, he could burn one of the feathers and Simurgh came to his aid.
A sword borrowed from Lü Dongbin to Xuanwu in order to subdue the spirits of the tortoise and the snake.
A magic flower that blooms on the eve of the Summer solstice. It will bring fortune to the person who finds it.
A wild fig tree that had religious and mythological significance in ancient Rome. The tree is associated with the legend of Romulus and Remus.
The fig is the edible fruit of Ficus carica (the common fig), a species of tree or shrub in the flowering plant family Moraceae, native to the Mediterranean region, and to western and southern Asia.
Adinkra symbol of the Akan people. Literal meaning: “The circular house”.
The sword of Garin de Monglane, formerly belonging to King Arthur. Mentioned together with Merveilleuse below.

Fire is one of the four classical elements along with earth, water and air in ancient Greek philosophy and science. Fire is considered to be both hot and dry and, according to Plato, is associated with the tetrahedron.
The feathers of a Firebird that glows brightly emitting red, orange, and yellow light, like a bonfire that is just past the turbulent flame.

The structure above the atmosphere, conceived as a vast solid dome according to the Biblical cosmology. According to the Genesis creation narrative, God created the firmament to separate the "waters above" the earth from the "waters below"…
A brew created by Meng Po that is given to each soul to drink before they leave Diyu. The brew induces instant and permanent amnesia, and all memory of other lives is lost.

entries.t: Five-colored jewel from a dragon's neck
entries.o: A jewel that shines five colors found in a dragon's neck. One of Kaguya-hime's suitor set out to search for the jewel.
Feather cloaks have been used by several cultures. It constituted noble and royal attire in § Hawaii and other Polynesian regions.
A symbol of Unitarian Universalism. Origin given: 1960s.
Oriental dragons are shown with a flaming pearl under their chin or in their claws. The pearl is associated with spiritual energy, wisdom, prosperity, power, immortality, thunder, or the moon.
A flaming sword is a sword which is glowing with a flame which is produced by some supernatural power.
A chariot drawn by deer.
Flight or flying is the motion of an object through an atmosphere or through the vacuum of space, in this case also called spaceflight, without contacting any planetary surface.
A flood is an overflow of water (or rarely other fluids) that submerges land that is usually dry. In the sense of "flowing water", the word may also be applied to the inflow of the tide.
Stories of overwhelming water frequently connect divine punishment and destruction with the survival of a remnant and a new beginning.
Impeded streams and removed blockages model some treatments of bodily suffering and reproductive difficulty in Turner’s account.
Flowers, also known as blossoms and blooms, are the reproductive structures of flowering plants. Typically, they are structured in four circular levels around the end of a stalk.

A magic carpet, also called a flying carpet, is a legendary carpet and common trope in fantasy fiction. It is typically used as a form of transportation and can quickly or instantaneously carry its user(s) to their destination.
A legendary ghost ship that can never make port and is doomed to sail the oceans forever.

entries.t: Flying mortar and pestle of Baba Yaga
entries.o: She flies around in a mortar and using the pestle as a rudder.
A supposed type of flying craft having a disc or saucer-shaped body, commonly used generically to refer to an anomalous flying object.
An eagle-propelled craft built by the Persian king Kay Kāvus. It was used for flying the king all the way to China.
Localized origin narratives describe the arrangement of landscapes, species and humanity through distinctive, sometimes humorous acts.
A type of UFO reported and named by the U.S. 415th Special Operations Squadron, the term was also commonly used to mean any UFO sighting from that period.
The foot (pl.: feet) is an anatomical structure found in many vertebrates. It is the terminal portion of a limb which bears weight and allows locomotion.
Eaten by Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, which they had been commanded not to do by God.

A forest is an ecosystem characterized by a dense community of trees. Hundreds of definitions of forest are used throughout the world, incorporating factors such as tree density, tree height, land use, legal standing, and ecological…
Dense, living growth figures the mysterious uncultivated world: a place of fear, wandering, fertility, and unexpected encounters.
A golden battle axe that Forseti (or Fosite in the Frisian mythology) used to save the old sages of the wreck and then threw the axe to an island to bring forth a source of water.
40 (forty) is the natural number following 39 and preceding 41. Though the word is related to four (4), the spelling forty replaced fourty during the 17th century and is now the standard form.

A fountain, from the Latin "fons" (genitive "fontis"), meaning source or spring, is a decorative reservoir used for discharging water. It is also a structure that jets water into the air for a decorative or dramatic effect in landscapes.
A spring that supposedly restores the youth of anyone who drinks or bathes in its waters.

4 (four) is a number, numeral and digit. It is the natural number following 3 and preceding 5. It is a square number, the smallest semiprime and composite number, and is considered unlucky in many East Asian cultures.
A concoction of vinegar infused with herbs, spices or garlic that was believed to protect the user from the plague (disease).

entries.t: Four Treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann
entries.o: Consisting of the Claíomh Solais, Lug's Spear, Cauldron of the Dagda, and the Lia Fáil.

The four-leaf clover is a rare mutation of the common three-leaf clover that has four leaflets instead of three. According to tradition, such clovers bring good luck, a belief that dates back to at least the 17th century.
A group or arrangement of four appears in some dream materials as an ordering pattern; its relevance has to be judged in that specific dream context.

Foxes are small-to-medium-sized omnivorous mammals belonging to several genera of the family Canidae. They have a flattened skull; upright, triangular ears; a pointed, slightly upturned snout; and a long, bushy tail ("brush").

In Irish mythology, Fragarach (or Freagarthach), known as "The Answerer" or "The Retaliator", was the sword of the sea god Manannán mac Lir. The sword weakened its foes, and no mail or armour could block it.
A chain of personal associations can uncover emotional connections, but Jung cautions that wandering away from the specific dream image can lose its distinctive significance.
A loosening of anxious attachment to personal fortune follows the recognition of one’s participation in a larger current of life.
A chariot pulled by cats.

(Frigg's distaff), the Orion's Belt asterism within the constellation of Orion was once known as "Frigg's Distaff". To explain this attribution, some scholars have pointed out that the constellation is on the celestial equator and thus the…

A flamberge (also floberge, froberge, and other variations) is a medieval sword that is swung by a number of fictional heroes of chansons de geste and romances, and the word became a generic name for a large sword.

A frog is any member of a diverse and largely semiaquatic group of short-bodied, tailless amphibian vertebrates composing the order Anura (coming from the Ancient Greek ἀνούρα, literally 'without tail').
Shells or pearls placed with the dead can be read as ritual signs of hoped-for re-creation rather than mere grave decoration, though contexts vary.
Adinkra symbol of the Akan people. Literal meaning: “Siamese crocodiles”. They share one stomach yet they fight over food

Fusang is a mythical world tree or place located far east of China. In the Classic of Mountains and Seas and several contemporary texts, the term refers to a mythological tree of life, alternatively identified as a mulberry or a hibiscus,…
(August-Snap-Spirit), the sword of Takemikazuchi.
The gada (Sanskrit: गदा gadā, Kannada: ಗದೆ, Telugu: గద, Tamil: கதை, Malay: gedak, Old Tagalog: batuta) is a mallet or blunt mace from the Indian subcontinent.
(Spear of Assal), another spear belonging to Lugh, the incantation "Ibar (Yew)" made the cast always hit its mark, and "Athibar (Re-Yew)" caused the spear to return.
A statue carved of ivory by Pygmalion of Cyprus, which the goddess Aphrodite brought to life before uniting the couple in marriage.

Gawain ( GA(H)-wayn, -⁠win, gə-WAYN), whose name is spelled in multiple ways, is one of the Knights of the Round Table in the Arthurian legendary cycle. His prototype appears under the name Gwalchmei in the earliest Welsh sources.
Gambanteinn is an Old Norse term referring to a magic staff or wand. It is attested in two poems in the Poetic Edda: Hárbarðsljóð and Skírnismál.
Gan Jiang (Chinese: 干將; pinyin: Gān Jiāng) and Mo Ye (Chinese: 莫邪; pinyin: Mò Yé) were a swordsmith couple, discussed in the literature involving the Spring and Autumn period of Chinese history.
Gandiva (IAST: Gāṇḍīva; Sanskrit: गाण्डीव) is a divine bow of Arjuna, one of the Pandavas from the Hindu epic Mahabharata. The bow was made by Brahma.

Ganesha, or Ganesh (Sanskrit: गणेश, IAST: Gaṇeśa, IPA: [ɡɐˈɳeːɕɐ]), also known as Ganapati, Vinayaka and Pillaiyar, is one of the best-known and most revered and worshipped deities in the Hindu pantheon and is the Supreme god in the…
Was a mythic Haoma plant that had healing properties and gave immortality to the resurrected bodies of the dead when eaten.

A garden is a planned space, usually outdoors, set aside for the cultivation, display, and enjoyment of plants and other forms of nature. The single feature identifying even the wildest wild garden is control.
An opening in a boundary makes visible entry, exclusion, invitation, and the possibility of crossing into another condition.
A legendary barrier supposedly built by Alexander the Great to keep the uncivilized barbarians of the north from invading the land to the south.
Various places on the surface of the world that have acquired a legendary reputation for being entrances to the underworld.
A gate flanked by adamantine columns, a substance so hard that nothing can cut through it, akin to diamond.
The Mayan god brought fire, earth, air, and water to the world. Kukulkan, though, only has the wind gem, and with it can control the air.

Gemini (♊︎; JEM-in-eye Greek: Δίδυμοι, romanized: Dídymoi, Latin for "twins") is the third astrological sign in the zodiac. Under the tropical zodiac, the sun transits this zodiac sign between about May 22 to June 21.
In folklore, a ghost is the soul or spirit of a dead person or non-human animal that is believed by some people to be able to appear to the living.
A ghost ship said to sail ablaze within the Northumberland Strait.
Siegfried takes her girdle which makes Brynhildr lose her supernatural strength.
In Greek mythology, Hippolyta, or Hippolyte (; Ancient Greek: Ἱππολύτη Hippolytē), was the queen of the Amazons and a daughter of Ares and Otrera. Her sisters were Antiope and Melanippe.
(Gjöll Bridge), a covered bridge which spans the river Gjöll and must be crossed in order to reach Hel.
In Norse mythology, Gjallarhorn (Old Norse: [ˈɡjɑlːɑrˌhorn]; "hollering horn" or "the loud sounding horn") is a horn associated with the god Heimdallr and the wise being Mímir.

Gjöll (Old Norse: Gjǫll [ˈɡjɔlː]) is the river that separates the living from the dead in Norse mythology. It is one of the eleven rivers traditionally associated with the Élivágar, rivers that existed in Ginnungagap at the beginning of…
(Gleaming), a tree or grove described as "the most beautiful among gods and men", bearing golden leaves located in the realm of Asgard, outside the doors of Valhalla.
In Norse mythology, Gleipnir (Old Norse "open one") is the binding that holds the mighty wolf Fenrir (as attested in chapter 34 of the Prose Edda book Gylfaginning).
A legendary Chinese sword allegedly forged in Tibet by husband-and-wife magicians of the ancient Bön tradition.
It could hold back the tide when it was thrown onto the seashore.
Gold, also called golden, is a color tone resembling the chemical element gold. The web color gold is sometimes referred to as golden to distinguish it from the color metallic gold.
A chain used by the deity Ọbatala to descend from the heavens so he could create the Earth.

Golden fruit from a tree that Earth gave to Hera as a wedding gift, growing in a garden at the western edge of the world and guarded by the nymphs of evening, the Hesperides, and a hundred-headed serpent.

A woodcutter accidentally dropped his axe into a river and sat down to weep. Hermes dived into the water and returned with a golden axe. Hermes asked if this is his axe, but the woodcutter said it was not.
Part of Fafnir's treasure which Sigurd took after he slew the dragon.
"The Goose that Laid the Golden Eggs" is one of Aesop's Fables, numbered 87 in the Perry Index, a story that also has a number of Eastern analogues.

The fleece of a winged golden ram, hung in a sacred grove in Colchis at the eastern end of the Black Sea and guarded by a dragon that never slept. Jason and the Argonauts sailed to win it, and with the help of the sorceress Medea they did.
Hephaestus gained revenge against Hera for rejecting him by making her a magical golden throne which when she sat on it, did not allow her to stand up.

An animated anthropomorphic being that is magically created entirely from inanimate matter (specifically clay or mud). The word was used to mean an amorphous, unformed material in Psalms and medieval writing.
Which was used by David to decapitate the fallen giant, and then given to him by the priest Achimelech when he ran away from King Shaul.

The cutting of the Gordian Knot is an ancient Greek legend associated with Alexander the Great in Gordium in Phrygia, regarding a complex knot that tied an oxcart. Reputedly, whoever could untie it would be destined to rule all of Asia.
An ox-headed mace described in various Iranian and Zoroastrian myths that is used as a symbol of victory and justice.

A golden mace wielded by Mithras, the god of covenants, that can be thrown from a distance, he twirls his mace over the heads of the demons every day and night in Hell to prevent them from harming the spirits of the dead too much.
The helmet of King Arthur, passed down to him from Uther Pendragon.
Three sisters who shared one eye among themselves.
A cracked holy sword which Sir Percival bonded back together, though the crack remained.
The search for restorative or extraordinary sustenance supplies one version of the larger boon pattern.
