The term "big cat" is sometimes used to mean any of the five living members of the genus Panthera (the tiger, lion, jaguar, leopard, and snow leopard), or may refer to any member of the cat family that is considered "big", such as cheetahs…

Great Goddess is the concept of an almighty goddess or mother goddess, or a matriarchal religion. These religions may have been Monotheistic, in which she was the singular deity, or Polytheistic in which she presided over a pantheon of…
Greco-Roman divine figures are identified in art by recognizable attributes and overlapping spheres of nature, society and human conduct.
Green is the color between cyan and yellow on the visible spectrum. It has 295–350 different shades. It is evoked by light which has a dominant wavelength of roughly 495–570 nm.

The Green Knight (Welsh: Marchog Gwyrdd, Cornish: Marghek Gwyrdh, Breton: Marc'heg Gwer) is a heroic character of the Matter of Britain, originating in the 14th-century poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and the related medieval work The…

The Green Dragon Crescent Blade (Chinese: 靑龍偃月刀) is a legendary weapon wielded by the Chinese general Guan Yu in the 14th-century historical novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms. It is a guandao, a type of traditional Chinese weapon.
The color green holds a distinct significance in Islamic culture, as it has appeared with symbolic meanings throughout various Islamic eras and among different schools and sects.
The Green Man, also known as a foliate head, is a motif in architecture and art, of a face made of, or completely surrounded by, foliage, which normally spreads out from the centre of the face.

The griffin, griffon, or gryphon (Ancient Greek: γρύψ, romanized: grýps; Classical Latin: gryps or grypus; Late and Medieval Latin: gryphes, grypho etc.; Old French: griffon) is a legendary creature with the body, tail, and back legs of a…
A large scythe wielded by the Grim Reaper.
The historical sword of Bolesław III Wrymouth, medieval prince of Poland.
Gríðr (Old Norse: [ˈɡriːðz̠]) often anglicized as Gríd, is a jötunn in Norse mythology. She is the mother of Víðarr the Silent and the consort of Óðinn. Saturn's moon Gridr was named after her.
Thomas Speght, an editor or Chaucer's works at the end of the 16th century, made a passing remark "Concerning Wade and his bote called Guingelot", and also his strange exploits in the same.
In Norse mythology, Gungnir (, "the rocker, the swaying one") is the spear of the god Odin. It is known for always hitting the target of the attacker regardless of the attacker's skill.
Gunnar's atgeir would make a ringing sound or "sing" when it was taken down in anticipation of bloodshed.
Magic arrows given to Örvar-Oddr by his father.

The unbreakable net that Ogun used to trap his wife Oya and her lover Shango when he caught them engaging in sexual activity. He subsequently dragged them, while still bound, before Olorun for judgement.
Adinkra symbol of the Akan people. Literal meaning: “The king's gun”.
Adinkra symbol of the Akan people. Literal meaning: “(In) the king's little eyes”. To be in the king's favour
An elderly woman who points Henry toward the path is read as a source of guidance outside his usual rational control.
Olifant (also known as oliphant) was the name applied in the Middle Ages to a type of carved ivory hunting horn created from elephant tusks.

The cultivated olive (botanical name Olea europaea subsp. europaea) is a subspecies of subtropical evergreen tree in the family Oleaceae. Modern cultivars are traced primarily to the Near East, Aegean Sea, and Strait of Gibraltar.

The olive branch, a ramus of Olea europaea, is a symbol of peace. It is generally associated with the customs of ancient Greece and ancient Rome, and is connected with supplication to divine beings and persons in power.

The most sacred sound and syllable in Hinduism, also central in Buddhism, Jainism and (as Ik Onkar) Sikhism. It is chanted at the beginning and end of prayers, readings and meditation, and written with the sign ॐ.
An omphalos is a religious stone artefact. In Ancient Greek, the word ὀμφᾰλός (omphalós) means "navel". Among the Ancient Greeks, it was a widespread belief that Delphi was the center of the world.
The cosmic staff of Ọbatala, king of the gods.
What the use of a symbol reveals: gestures, treatment of participants, emotional tone, roles and exclusions in the actual performance.
In lexical semantics, opposites are words lying in an inherently incompatible binary relationship. For example, something that is even entails that it is not odd.
A metal that was considered second only to gold in value, and was mined in Atlantis in ancient times.
The sword of the Fomorian king Tethra, which recounts the deeds done with it when unsheathed. It was taken by Ogma and it then recounted everything it had done.

An orphan is a child whose parents have died, are unknown, or have permanently abandoned them. The Shorter Oxford English Dictionary, 3rd edition, defines the term: "One deprived by death of father or mother, or (usu.) of both; a…
In Greek mythology, Orpheus ( ; Ancient Greek: Ὀρφεύς, classical pronunciation: [or.pʰeú̯s]) was a Thracian bard, legendary musician and prophet.
A golden lyre given to him by Apollo. It is said that Orpheus' music and singing could charm the birds, fish and wild beasts, coax the trees and rocks into dance, and divert the course of rivers.
A mirror that the river spirit Oshun keeps upon her person and uses as her symbol as the goddess of beauty.
Oshé (Yoruba alphabet: Oṣé) is the double-headed battle axe of the thunder deity Ṣango in Yoruba religion, sometimes considered to be representing bolts of lightning hurled by the deity from Ọrun.
Osiris (, from Egyptian wsjr) was the god of fertility, agriculture, the afterlife, the dead, resurrection, life, and vegetation in ancient Egyptian religion.

A beautifully carved coffin made by Set. Osiris was tricked by Set to enter the chest, and was enclosed inside it by 72 accomplices of Set. Set flung the coffer in the Nile so that it would drift far away.

Touken Ranbu Hanamaru (Japanese: 刀剣乱舞-花丸-) is a Japanese anime television series produced by Doga Kobo and Toho, directed by Takashi Naoya and written by Pierre Sugiura, with character designs by Junichiro Taniguchi and music composed by…

A serpent or dragon that swallows its own tail, forming a circle with no beginning or end. From Egyptian tombs to Greek alchemy, Norse myth and modern psychology, it stands for eternity, the cycle of destruction and renewal, and the unity…

Owls are birds from the order Strigiformes (), which includes over 200 species of mostly solitary and nocturnal birds of prey typified by an upright stance, a large, broad head, binocular vision, binaural hearing, sharp talons, and…
Adinkra symbol of the Akan people. Literal meaning: “The symbol of heroic deeds and accomplishing the impossible, but being quiet about it”.

Oyster is the common name for a number of different families of salt-water bivalve molluscs that live in marine or brackish habitats. In some species, the valves are highly calcified, and many are somewhat irregular in shape.
The bow wielded by the divine hunter Oṣosi.
Adinkra symbol of the Akan people. Literal meaning: “To strike fire (with a flint)”.
(Cauldron of Rebirth), a magical cauldron able to revive the dead.
A wooden statue that fell from the sky. As long as it stayed in Troy, the city-state could not lose a war.
The Arecaceae () are a family of perennial, flowering plants in the monocot order Arecales. Their growth form can be climbers, shrubs, tree-like and stemless plants, all commonly known as palms.
A pan flute (also known as panpipes or syrinx) is a musical instrument based on the principle of the closed tube, consisting of multiple pipes of gradually increasing length (and occasionally girth).
A pan flute (also known as panpipes or syrinx) is a musical instrument based on the principle of the closed tube, consisting of multiple pipes of gradually increasing length (and occasionally girth).
A remedy that would cure all diseases and prolong life indefinitely.
Panchajanya (Sanskrit: पाञ्चजन्य, IAST: Pāñcajanya) is the shankha (conch) of the Hindu preserver deity Vishnu, one of his four primary attributes.
Pandora's box is an artefact in Greek mythology connected with the myth of Pandora in Hesiod's c. 700 B.C. poem Works and Days.
An axe wielded by Pangu. He used it to separate yin from yang, creating the Earth (murky yin) and the Sky (clear yang).

A legendary torture device created by the wicked fox spirit Daji. It was a tall bronze cylinder heated with charcoal, but if one fell off they would die. With no other alternatives one was forced to dance atop the cylinder until they died.
Adinkra symbol of the Akan people. Literal meaning: “The (large number of) people who do good prevents us knowing who really are Mohammedans”.
Parashu (Sanskrit: Paraśu) is the Sanskrit word for a battle-axe, which can be wielded with one or both hands.

The chatra or chhatra, also known under various translations including the ceremonial, state, royal, or holy umbrella or parasol, is a symbol of royal and imperial power and sanctity in Indian art and a symbol of holiness in Hinduism,…

A parazonium is a long triangular dagger, wide at the hilt end and coming to a point. In Roman iconography, it is frequently carried by Virtus, particularly in early representations of the deity, Mars, and Dea Roma, as well as the emperor,…

A pasha (Sanskrit: पाश, romanized: pāśa, lit. 'noose, lasso') is a supernatural weapon depicted in Hindu iconography. Hindu deities such as Ganesha, Yama, Shyamala devi, and Varuna are depicted with the pasha in their hands.

The Pashupatastra (IAST: Pāśupatāstra, Sanskrit: पाशुपतास्त्र; the Pashupati, an epithet of Shiva) is an astra, a celestial missile, affiliated with the Hindu deity Shiva, as well as Kali and Adi Parashakti, which can be discharged by the…
A path offers direction and possibility while every turning point exposes choice, uncertainty, and future change.
The divine sword of the Veerabhadra, a commander of Shiva's troops.
An axe wielded by Paul Bunyan. It was responsible for carving the Grand Canyon after Paul once dragged it behind him while walking.

The peach (Prunus persica) is a deciduous tree that bears edible juicy fruits with various characteristics. Most are simply called peaches, while the glossy-skinned, non-fuzzy varieties are called nectarines.

In Chinese mythology, Peaches of Immortality (Chinese: 仙桃; pinyin: xiāntáo; Cantonese Yale: sīn tòuh or Chinese: 蟠桃; pinyin: pántáo; Cantonese Yale: pùhn tòuh) are consumed by the immortals due to their mystic virtue of conferring…

The peacock was the patron bird of the Goddess Hera. According to myth, she adorned the tail of a peacock with Argus's eyes on its feathers in his honor, symbolizing all-seeing knowledge and the wisdom of the heavens.
Gnostic and Christian narratives reconfigure the costly, hidden pearl as spiritual knowledge, redemption or an otherwise inaccessible treasure.
A conceptual entry to Heaven.
Pegasus (Ancient Greek: Πήγασος, romanized: Pḗgasos; Latin: Pegasus, Pegasos) is a winged horse in Greek mythology, usually depicted as a white stallion.

Pelicans (genus Pelecanus) are a genus of large water birds that make up the family Pelecanidae. They are characterized by a long beak and a large throat pouch used for catching prey and draining water from the scooped-up contents before…

Which Odysseus's wife Penelope pretended to weave for her deceased father-in-law. She claimed that she would choose a suitor when the shroud was complete, but secretly unraveled it every night to delay the decision.

A pentacle (also spelled and pronounced as pantacle in Thelema, following Aleister Crowley, though that spelling ultimately derived from Éliphas Lévi) is a talisman that is used in magical evocation, and is usually made of parchment,…

A pentagram (sometimes known as a pentalpha, pentangle, or star pentagon) is a regular five-pointed star polygon, formed from the diagonal line segments of a convex (or simple, or non-self-intersecting) regular pentagon.

In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Persephone ( Ancient Greek: Περσεφόνη) is the daughter of Zeus and Demeter. She became the queen of the underworld after her abduction by her uncle Hades, the king of the underworld, who later took…
Age, personality, life circumstances, feelings, and the dreamer’s own responses can change the reading of outwardly similar dreams.
Peter claimed that the Devil had given him a magical belt or girdle, which enabled him to metamorphose into a werewolf. Removing the belt made him transform back to his human form.
In the Odyssey, are described as being as fast as a falcon, steered by thought and requiring no helmsman, and able to travel even through mist or fog without any danger of being shipwrecked.

An hypothetical planet hypothesized by the Titius–Bode law to have existed between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter, the destruction of which supposedly led to the formation of the asteroid belt (including the dwarf planet Ceres).

A funeral train decorated in black bunting said to run regularly from Washington, D.C. to Springfield, Illinois, around the anniversary of Abraham Lincoln's death, stopping watches and clocks in surrounding areas as it passes.

Pheme is the goddess of gossip and she was said to have pried into the affairs of mortals and gods. She then repeated what she had learned by sounding her trumpet to spread the gossip to people near and far.
The legendary substance of the alchemists that could turn base metals like lead into gold and, many believed, heal diseases and lengthen life as an elixir. Making it was the Great Work (magnum opus).
A legendary bird that lives for centuries and is reborn from its own death: in the best-known version, it builds a nest of spices, bursts into flame and rises young again from the ashes.
An amulet or charm, worn for its supposed magical power.
Which the Pied Piper used to lure the rats, and later children, out of Hamelin.

The pig (Sus domesticus), also called swine (pl.: swine) or hog, is an omnivorous, domesticated, even-toed, hoofed mammal. It is named the domestic pig when distinguishing it from other members of the genus Sus.
Four pillars held Heaven and the goddess Nüwa repaired the pillars after the time when Heaven and Earth were in disruption.
Lot's wife was turned into a pillar of salt when she looked back at the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah as they were destroyed.
Hercules raised two pillars at the Strait of Gibraltar when he passed by during one of his ten labours. The tenth labour was to obtain the Cattle of Geryon.

The Pinaka (Sanskrit: पिनाक, pināka) is the celestial bow of the Hindu deity, Shiva. In popular legend, he is believed to have employed this bow in his avatar as Tripurantaka to annihilate the three cities of Mayasura, known as Tripura.
Pisces (♓︎; ; Ancient Greek: Ἰχθύες Ikhthyes, Latin for "fishes") is the twelfth and final astrological sign in the zodiac. It is a mutable sign. It spans 330° to 360° of celestial longitude.
A hypothetical fifth terrestrial planet posited by NASA scientists John Chambers and Jack J. Lissauer to have once existed between Mars and the asteroid belt.
A hypothetical planet, now disproven, proposed in 1906 by Percival Lowell to have existed beyond the planet Neptune.
Visible wandering heavenly bodies acquire names and characteristics of gods and structure traditional astrology.
Free movement within rules or imagination creates a space of experiment, spontaneity, and imaginative transformation.
A myth may answer different questions depending on its social, psychological, religious or poetic reading; none necessarily exhausts it.

A supernatural substance that is present in all souls and sustains life in all breathing living creatures. Thought of as giving cosmic energy through breath. One main components of the parts of the soul in ancient Greek medicine.
Featured frequently in folktales or fairy tales.

a: Fruit of the Dead in Greek mythology
entries.o: A red fruit full of hundreds of jewel-like seeds: in Greek myth the fruit that bound Persephone to the underworld; in the Bible, the ornament of the high priest's robe and Solomon's Temple; in Christian art, a sign of the Resurrection and…
Pulled by hippocampi.
Significance emerging from a symbol’s juxtaposition with other images and actions in a particular ritual configuration.
Which is used by leprechauns to store away all their coins at the end of the rainbow.
Hands transforming soft earth into a vessel echo creation stories and the shaping of a bounded individual form.
Is all cosmic energy, permeating the Universe on all levels. Prana is often referred to as the "life force" or "life energy". It also includes energies present in inanimate objects.

Pranayama (Sanskrit: प्राणायाम, "Prāṇāyāma") is the yogic practice of controlling the breath in Hinduism. It is described in Hindu texts such as the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita; in the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, it is one of the eight…
Pridwen was, according to the 12th-century writer Geoffrey of Monmouth, King Arthur's shield; it was adorned with an image of the Virgin Mary.

Is the ubiquitous starting material required for the alchemical magnum opus and the creation of the philosopher's stone. It is the primitive formless base of all matter similar to chaos, the quintessence, or aether.
A not-yet-ordinary being acts in the fluid early world, before mythic origin passes into human chronology.
An undivided source that is narrated as becoming a multiplicity of distinguishable forms.
A person may unknowingly attribute an inner concern or quality to an external figure or event, obscuring its personal psychological contribution.
Unbreakable shackles of adamantine that were made by Hephaestus and broken by Heracles.
Staff belonging to the wizard Prospero in the Shakespearean play "The Tempest.".
A carried sign or enchanted object expresses the possibility of assistance beyond one’s ordinary resources.

In Greek mythology, Proteus ( PROH-tee-əs, PROHT-yooss; Ancient Greek: Πρωτεύς, romanized: Prōteús) is an early prophetic sea god or god of rivers and oceanic bodies of water, one of several deities whom Homer calls the "Old Man of the…

Précieuse (French for 'precious'; Old French: Preciuse) is the sword of Baligant, the Saracen king in the French epic The Song of Roland. Baligant allegedly named his sword in response to hearing that Charlemagne's sword had a name.
Campbell examines the relation between mythic cosmology and psychological interpretations, without equating every religious claim with a fact about physics.
Giving voice to hidden resentments in a communal healing ceremony can reorder strained relationships as part of the ritual’s purpose.
Purple is a color similar in appearance to violet light. In the RYB color model historically used in the arts, purple is a secondary color created by combining red and blue pigments.
A powerful magic gourd that sucks anyone who speaks before it inside and melts them down into a bloody stew.
Metamorphic obstacles and evasions make the bearer’s contested passage away from a supernatural domain vivid.

(An Aeroplane with flowers), a mythical Aeroplane found in Ayyavazhi mythology. In Maharashtra, it is the Pushpak Viman (a heavenly aircraft shaped as an eagle) which took Saint Tukaram (a devotee of Vishnu) to heaven.

Vimāna are mythological flying palaces or chariots described in Hindu texts and Sanskrit epics. The "Pushpaka Vimana" of Ravana (who took it from Kubera; Rama returned it to Kubera) is the most quoted example of a vimana.

A belief that the ancient Egyptian pyramids and objects of similar shape can confer a variety of benefits. Among these assumed properties are the ability to preserve foods, sharpen or maintain the sharpness of razor blades, etc.
An active principle forming part of any living thing. Qi literally translates as "breath", "air", or "gas", and figuratively as "material energy", "life force", or "energy flow".
One of the ten ancient artifacts, the universe bag or cosmos bag is a bag belonging to Maitreya that is able to fit all of heaven and earth inside.
A four-part arrangement can structure images of order or completion, especially when organized around a center.

Quetzalcoatl () (Nahuatl: "Feathered Serpent") is a deity in Aztec culture and literature. Among the Aztecs, he was related to wind, the planet Venus, the Sun, merchants, arts, crafts, knowledge, and learning.
The foot of a rabbit is carried as an amulet believed to bring good luck.
A symbol of Roman imperial cult. Origin given: 2nd century CE.

A radiant or radiate crown, also known as a solar crown, sun crown, Eastern crown, or tyrant's crown, is a crown, wreath, diadem, or other headgear symbolizing the Sun or more generally powers associated with the Sun.

When King Ælla threw Ragnar into the snake pit, it was claimed Ragnar was protected by an enchanted shirt that Aslaug had made. It was only when this shirt had been removed that the snakes could bite Ragnar and kill him.
Drawn by eight black horses.
Rain or rainfall is a form of atmospheric precipitation composed of droplets of water aerosols that have condensed from atmospheric water vapor and fall by gravity.

The rainbow has been a favorite component of mythology throughout history among many cultures around the world. Abrahamic traditions see it as a covenant with God to preserve the world from a second flood.
A floating bridge across the sea constructed by the apes Nala and Nila in the epic poem Ramayana.
A magical herb which can unlock or uncover anything that is locked or closed.
A drill or auger that was used by Odin during his quest to obtain the mead of poetry.
(Book of Power), a legendary book about black magic, alleged to have been buried with its author, the Bishop Gottskálk grimmi Nikulásson of Holar.
A raven is any of several large-bodied passerine bird species in the genus Corvus. These species do not form a single taxonomic group within the genus.
A return to life in myth or rite can express psychological renewal after an ordeal, loss, or surrender.
Red is the color at the long wavelength end of the visible spectrum of light, next to orange and opposite violet. It has a dominant wavelength of approximately 625–750 nanometers.

An East Asian belief originating from Chinese legend. According to this myth, the gods tie an invisible red cord around the ankles of those that are destined to meet one another in a certain situation or help each other in a certain way.
The prospective traveler resists an unsettling summons, leaving familiar aims or defenses in command.
After an extraordinary realization, the hero may prefer not to resume the demands and limits of common life.
(Old Norse God Nails), are nails used for religious purposes.
Breaking restraints can signify rescue from harmful power or a restoration of life, dramatized in myths and prayers for divine release.

entries.t: Relic of the tooth of the Buddha
entries.o: Venerated in Sri Lanka as a cetiya "relic" of Gautama Buddha, the founder of Buddhism.
A number of relics associated with Jesus that have been claimed and displayed throughout the history of Christianity.
An ally or intervention from the ordinary world helps the traveler recover from a realm difficult to leave unaided.
Re-entry into everyday or communal existence with the consequences of the extraordinary encounter.
An often neglected second boundary: the task is to bring altered insight into a world whose old expectations remain.
Drawn by lions.
A hoard of gold in the Nibelungenlied where three Rheinmaidens swim and protect the treasure.
Rhongomyniad, or Rhongomiant (variously translated as "Slaying Spear," "Cutting Spear" or "Striking Spear"), was the spear of King Arthur in the Welsh Arthurian legends.
A portable circle materializes bonds, promises, wholeness, and an enduring relation, while sometimes implying enclosure.

A ring given to Sir Lancelot by the Lady of the Lake which could dispel any enchantment. In Le Chevalier de la Charrette it is given to him by a fairy instead. He used the ring to cross the Sword Bridge.

g: Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
entries.o: Eluned's stone and ring (Lunete's ring) come from the prose tale Owain, or the Lady of the Fountain. The "Three Treasures" text itself explained that it was the ring that the girl Eluned gave to Owain son of Urien (Ywain ap Urien) when he…

A gold ring that makes its wearer invisible when its bezel is turned inward: the centre of a thought experiment in Plato's Republic. A shepherd who finds it uses it to seduce a queen, kill a king and seize a throne.
The ring that Gonzalo Gustioz breaks in two pieces to so he can later on recognize the son with which his lover is pregnant.
Separation from an earlier status, an ambiguous margin, and eventual incorporation provide the comparative frame Turner adopts from van Gennep.
Turner analyzes ritual activity as expressive of friction within collective obligations: a symbol of solidarity can also stage a confrontation.
A practitioner competent in specific cult procedures, often someone whose own earlier affliction qualified them for a healing role.
During the margin of transition novices may learn norms through striking displays, discipline and explanations of ritually important objects.
The people who organize, finance and control Mukanda can use ritual roles to negotiate prestige and tensions between villages and kin groups.
For Turner an object, act or image becomes symbolically meaningful within an enacted web of social relations, affect and indigenous explanation.
Rites address illnesses, reproductive difficulty or hunting failure attributed locally to a deceased relative’s shade; the patient may later become an adept.
A river is a natural stream of fresh water that flows on land or inside caves towards another body of water at a lower elevation, such as an ocean, lake, or another river.

Norse mythology contains references to various named weapons wielded by specific characters. The oldest references sometimes offer nothing except a name for the weapon, but some of them include more detail on the weapon and what makes it…
The adventurer meets repeated ordeals whose accumulated effects transform ability and understanding.
A legendary robe of China that is made of the fireproof fur of the fire-rat. One of Kaguya-hime's suitor set out to search for the robe.

A plain staff with a single snake coiled around it, carried by Asclepius, the Greek god of healing. It is the true traditional emblem of medicine, used by the World Health Organization, many national medical associations and the "Star of…
What grows unseen below supports visible life; roots evoke ancestry, nourishment, hidden origins, and attachment to place.

Various folk cultures and traditions assign symbolic meaning to the rose, though these are seldom understood in-depth. Examples of deeper meanings lie within the language of flowers, and how a rose may have a different meaning in…

Rose window is often used as a generic term applied to a circular window, but is especially used for those found in Gothic cathedrals and churches. The windows are divided into segments by stone mullions and tracery.
(lit. Rowing Wheel), the magical flying machine of Mug Ruith, a mythological Irish Druid who along with his feathered headdress (the encennach), hovers across the skies .
King Arthur's famed table, around which he and his Knights congregate. As its name suggests, it has no head, implying that everyone who sits there has equal status.
Magical staff wielded by the Monkey King Sun Wukong in the Chinese classic novel, Journey to the West.
The Rub el Hizb (Arabic: رُبُع الْحِزْب or رُبْع الْحِزْب rubʿ al-ḥizb 'quarter of the party') is an Islamic symbol in the shape of an octagram, represented as two overlapping squares ۞.

Ruyi Jingu Bang (Chinese: 如意金箍棒; pinyin: Rúyì Jīngū Bàng; Wade–Giles: Ju2-yi4 Chin1-ku1-pang4), or simply Ruyi Bang or Jingu Bang, is the poetic name of a magical staff wielded by the immortal monkey Sun Wukong in the 16th-century classic…

A ruyi (Chinese: 如意; pinyin: Rúyì; lit. 'as desired', 'as [you] wish') is a Chinese curved decorative object that serves as either a ceremonial scepter in Chinese Buddhism or a talisman symbolizing power and good fortune in Chinese…
(Dragon Palace Castle), undersea palace of Ryūjin, the dragon god of the sea. Depending on the version of the legend, it is built from red and white coral, or from solid crystal.
A net in which she tried to capture men who ventured out on the sea. Her net is also mentioned in Reginsmál and in the Völsunga saga, where she lends it to Loki so that he can capture Andvari.

The red cap of the Saci which is the said source of all his magical abilities, like appearing and disappearing at will, inhuman speed (despite having just one leg) and the power to create and ride dust devils.
Climbing a sacred tree, ladder or mountain dramatizes an encounter with a level of being inaccessible in ordinary space.
A cloak believed to have been worn by the Islamic prophet Muhammad.
Fire around the Mukanda site helps organize separation and ritual stages, providing a visible focus for boundaries and interaction.

The Most Sacred Heart of Jesus (Latin: Cor Jesu Sacratissimum) is one of the most widely practised and well-known Catholic devotions, wherein the heart of Jesus Christ is viewed as a symbol of "God's boundless and passionate love for…

Euhemerus (; also spelled Euemeros or Evemerus; Ancient Greek: Εὐήμερος, romanized: Euhēmeros, lit. 'happy' or 'prosperous'; late fourth century BC) was a Greek mythographer at the court of Cassander, the king of Macedon.
Consist of religious pieces sent to the Ottoman Sultans between the 16th century to the late 19th century.
A source of life or extraordinary nourishment that corresponds with entering the deepest generative center.
Stones may be treated as enduring presences or as sites of religious power when a community invests them with sacred meaning.
A sacred tree located at the Temple at Uppsala, Sweden, in the second half of the 11th century. It is not known what species it was, but a scholar has suggested that it was a yew tree.
An inhabited, ritually ordered territory is imagined as a meaningful cosmos distinguished from the dangerous, unknown outside.
Sagitta is a dim but distinctive constellation in the northern sky. Its name is Latin for 'arrow', not to be confused with the significantly larger constellation Sagittarius 'the archer'.

Sagittarius (♐︎; Ancient Greek: Τοξότης, romanized: Toxótēs, Latin for "archer") is the ninth astrological sign, which is associated with the constellation Sagittarius and spans 240–70th degrees of the zodiac.

entries.t: Saintly Crossbow of the Supernaturally Luminous Golden Claw
a: SV: Linh Quang Kim Trảo Thần Nỏ
entries.o: Which could kill 300 men with one shot. A giant golden turtle (also Kim Quy) gave An Dương Vương one of his claws and instructed him to make a crossbow using it as a trigger, assuring him he would be invincible with it.

The Salmon of Knowledge (Irish: An Bradán Feasa) is a creature in the Fenian Cycle of Irish mythology, sometimes identified with the mythical seer Fintan mac Bóchra who was known as "The Wise" and was once transformed into a salmon.
A magic object of Finnish epic poetry, forged by the smith Ilmarinen, that grinds out grain, salt and money without end and brings prosperity to whoever holds it.

The Sandals of Jesus Christ were among the most important relics of the Catholic Church in the Middle Ages. They were donated to Prüm Abbey by Pepin the Short who received them from Pope Stephen II (752–757).
Which the Sandman uses to put people to sleep and bring good dreams by sprinkling it into their eyes while they sleep.
A magical herb which can cure any malady. It was believed that medicines prepared from this herb could revive a dead person.

Sankofa (pronounced SAHN-koh-fah) is a word in the Akan language of Ghana meaning "to retrieve" (literally "go back and get"; san - to return; ko - to go; fa - to fetch, to seek and take) This Adinkra symbol is represented either with a…
Carries a bag full of presents for children.

In traditional Western festive legend and popular culture, Santa Claus's reindeer are said to pull a sleigh through the night sky to help Santa Claus deliver gifts to children during the night between Christmas Eve and Christmas Day.
The legendary workshop where Santa Claus is said to make the toys and presents, given out at Christmas.
Themis was portrayed carrying scales.

Anubis weighed the person's heart on a scale against the feather of Maat. If the heart is lighter than the feather, the person is allowed to pass into the afterlife. If not, the heart is eaten by Ammit.
Scales signal measured fairness and judgment, appearing in both civic allegory and scenes that weigh the dead.

Lady Justice (Latin: Iustitia) is an allegorical personification of the moral force in judicial systems. Her attributes are scales, a sword and sometimes a blindfold. She often appears as a pair with Prudentia.
Scarabs are amulets and impression seals shaped according to the eponymous beetles, which were widely popular throughout ancient Egypt.
A sceptre (spelled scepter in American English) is a staff or wand held in the hand by a ruling monarch as an item of royal or imperial insignia, signifying sovereign authority.

Scorpio (♏︎; Ancient Greek: Σκορπιός, romanized: Skorpiós, Latin for "scorpion") is the eighth astrological sign in the zodiac, originating from the constellation of Scorpius. It spans 210–240° ecliptic longitude.
During the Renaissance, Father Time was depicted as wielding the harvesting scythe, and became the representative of the cruel and unrelenting flow of time which, in the end, cuts down all things.

entries.t: Se die fofoo pe, ne se gyinantwi abo bedie
entries.o: Adinkra symbol of the Akan people. Literal meaning: “What the yellow-flowered fofoo plant wants is that the gyinantwi seeds should turn black”. An Asante saying. One of the cotton cloth designs bears the same name.
A sea is a very large body of salty water. The term has two distinct meanings. The first is the interconnected body of seawater that spans most of Earth, known as the sea or the ocean.
The magic signet ring of King Solomon, engraved with a divine name or a star, which gave him power over demons and jinn and, in Islamic tradition, the speech of animals and command of the wind.

The Seamless Robe of Jesus (also known as the Holy Robe, Holy Tunic, Holy Coat, Honorable Robe, and Chiton of the Lord) is the robe said to have been worn by Jesus during or shortly before his crucifixion.
A seashell (or sea shell), also known simply as a shell, is a hard, protective outer layer usually created by an animal or organism that lives in the sea.
The seasonal cycle orders agricultural and religious time, often dramatizing decline and return through myths of vegetation.
The sword that Lancelot used to battle the Saxons at Saxon Rock. It is translated as Seure (Sequence) in the Vulgate Cycle.

Seclusion is the act of secluding (i.e. isolating from society), the state of being secluded, or a place that facilitates it (a secluded place). A person, couple, or larger group may go to a secluded place for privacy or peace and quiet.
According to Latter Day Saint theology, seer stones were used by Joseph Smith, as well as ancient prophets, to receive revelations from God.
(counting, enumeration) the kabbalistic tree of life which encompasses both the physical and higher metaphysical realm. It consists of the ten attributes/emanations in Kabbalah.
Drawn across the night sky by her bulls or horses.
In philosophy, the self is an individual's own being, knowledge, and values, and the relationship between these attributes. The first-person perspective distinguishes selfhood from personal identity.
Selkies are said to live as seals in the sea but shed their skin to become human on land. If a man steals a female selkie's skin, she is in his power and is forced to become his wife.
The symbol’s meanings associated with observable or bodily qualities that provoke affect, such as milky latex, blood and sensations.
The division of once-joined cosmic regions makes an inhabitable world and its directions intelligible.
Adinkra symbol of the Akan people. Literal meaning: “A knife thrust through the cheeks of a man”. The man is about to be executed to prevent his invoking of a curse on the king
(Growing Weaker), the second six hours of the day (from noon till dusk) in Ancient Egyptian belief. It was preceded by the Matet boat.

The serpent, or snake, is one of the oldest and most widespread mythological symbols. The word is derived from Latin serpens, a crawling animal or snake. Snakes have been associated with some of the oldest rituals known to humankind.
The Sessho-seki (殺生石, Sesshōseki), or "Killing Stone", is a stone in the volcanic mountains of Nasu, an area of Tochigi Prefecture, Japan, that is famous for sulphurous hot springs.
Is both the goddess Freyja's hall located in Fólkvangr, a field where Freyja receives half of those who die in battle, and also the name of a ship.

7 (seven) is the natural number following 6 and preceding 8. It is the only prime number preceding a cube. As an early prime number in the series of positive integers, the number seven has symbolic associations in religion, mythology,…

Seven angels are thus given seven bowls of God's wrath, each consisting of judgements full of the wrath of God. These seven bowls of God's wrath are poured out on the wicked and the followers of the Antichrist after the sounding of the…
A Christian moral scheme personifies recurrent vices as figures or narrative episodes, furnishing material for allegorical art.
The Buddha’s seven birth-steps are interpreted through an image of crossing the structured cosmos and transcending the ordinary conditions of existence.
Seven angels with seven trumpets are sounded and the events that follow are described in detail from Revelation Chapters 8 to 11.

Seven golden trumpets, each of which was connected to one of the seven realms of the world, and by blowing each of those trumpets, Zahhak would send down deadly disasters such as plagues, earthquakes, and rain of fire on that land.
Seven-league boots are an element in European folklore. The boots allow the person wearing them to take strides of seven leagues per step, resulting in great speed.
In Ndembu belief a deceased relative may trouble living kin who neglect memory or obligation; appeasement may renew their relationship and initiate ritual vocation.
A shadow is a dark area on a surface where light from a light source is blocked by an object. In contrast, shade occupies the three-dimensional volume behind an object with light in front of it.
A plant honored as sacred by ancient Druids. The Druids believed the shamrock had the power to avert evil spirits. Some people still believe the shamrock has mystical, even prophetic powers.
Shamshir-e Zomorrodnegār (Persian: شمشیر زمردنگار, 'the emerald-studded sword') is a sword mentioned in the Persian epic the Shahnameh. It was said to have originally belonged to King Solomon.

A Shankha (Sanskrit: शङ्ख, romanized: śaṅkha, lit. 'conch') has religious ritual importance in Hinduism. In Hinduism, the shankha called panchajanya is a sacred emblem of the Hindu preserver deity Vishnu.
In mythology, folklore and speculative fiction, shapeshifting is the ability to physically transform oneself through unnatural means.
Sharnga (Sanskrit: शार्ङ्ग, romanized: Śārṅga) also spelled as Saranga or Sharanga, is the celestial bow of the Hindu god Vishnu, primarily associated with his avatar of Rama.
Sharur (Sumerian:𒊹𒃡 šar₂-ur₃), which means "smasher of thousands" is the weapon and symbol of the god Ninurta. Sumerian mythic sources describe it as an enchanted talking mace.

A sheela na gig is a figurative carving of a naked woman displaying an exaggerated vulva. These carvings, from the Middle Ages, are architectural grotesques found throughout most of Europe on cathedrals, castles, and other buildings.
The alleged wife of Saint Patrick who would sweep the winter away and gives one last snowstorm after Saint Patrick's Day.
A protective form made by a water creature connects enclosure to generation, feminine mysteries, and the distant sea.
The shield of Achilles is the shield that Achilles uses in his fight with Hector, as described in a passage in Book 18, lines 478–608 of Homer's Iliad.
The shield that Aeneas receives from Vulcan to aid in his war against Turnus.
A huge shield made of seven cow-hides with a layer of bronze.
A shield which bears the image of a fierce shining golden dragon.
A white shield belonging to King Evalach. Josephus of Arimathea painted a red cross upon it with his own blood, which granted the owner heavenly protection. It was later won by Sir Galahad.
The Shield of Heracles (Ancient Greek: Ἀσπὶς Ἡρακλέους, Aspis Hērakleous) is an archaic Greek epic poem that was attributed to Hesiod during antiquity.
According to Arthurian legend, was carried by three maidens to Arthur's castle where it was discovered by Sir Percival. In Perlesvaus he uses it to defeat the Knight of the Burning Dragon.
A red shield emblazoned with a golden eagle. According to Arthurian legend the same shield was later found and used by Gawain after he defeated an evil knight.
Shimenawa (標縄/注連縄/七五三縄, lit. 'enclosing rope') are lengths of laid rice straw or hemp rope used for ritual purification in the Shinto religion.
A ship is a large watercraft designed for travel across the surface of a body of water, carrying cargo or passengers, or in support of specialized tasks such as warfare, oceanography and fishing.
The ship Theseus rode on his trip to kill Minotaur. He set off with a black sail, promising to his father, Aegeus, that if successful he would return with a white sail.
A shipwreck is the wreckage of a ship that is either beached on land or sunken to the bottom of a body of water. It results from the event of shipwrecking, which may be intentional or unintentional.
Kappas can gain power by taking human's shirikodama, a mythical ball said to contain the soul.

In Greek mythology, the Shirt of Nessus, Tunic of Nessus, Nessus-robe, or Nessus' shirt (Ancient Greek: Χιτών τοῦ Νέσσου, romanized: Chitṓn toû Néssou) was the poisoned shirt (chiton) that killed Heracles.

Shiva (; Sanskrit: शिव, IAST: Śiva, lit. 'The Auspicious One'), also known as Mahadeva (; Sanskrit: महादेव, IAST: Mahādevaḥ, [mɐɦaːd̪eːʋɐh], lit. 'The Great God') and Hara, is one of the principal deities of Hinduism.
The Hindu God Shiva wears two earrings or Kundalas. Traditional images of Shiva depict the two earrings named – Alakshya and Niranjana.
A lingam (IAST: liṅga, lit. "sign, symbol or mark"), sometimes referred to as linga or Shiva linga, is an abstract or aniconic representation of the Hindu god Shiva in Shaivism.
It could burn even gods to ashes.
Which gave the god Vidar unparalleled foot protection.
A shofar ( shoh-FAR; from שׁוֹפָר, pronounced [ʃoˈfar] ) is an ancient musical horn, typically a ram's horn, used for Jewish ritual purposes.
(German Dreikönigsschrein), a reliquary said to contain the bones of the Biblical Magi, also known as the Three Kings or the Three Wise Men.
A length of linen cloth bearing the image of a man, is believed by some to be the burial shroud of Jesus of Nazareth.
Described to have helped Rome in many situations.
A failing ruler in a tale may portray a crisis of psychic organization that calls for an unfamiliar restorative task.
(The Perilous Seat), a vacant seat at the Round Table reserved by Merlin for the knight who would one day be successful in the quest for the Holy Grail.
A symbol of Satanism. Origin given: 1960s.
A sign is an object, quality, event, or entity whose presence or occurrence indicates the probable presence or occurrence of something else.

Similar to mana or ether, the primary component of everything that exists; it is also the breath of life and the method of locomotion for any movement or change. Silla was believed to control everything that goes on in one's life.

Silence is the absence of ambient audible sound, the emission of sounds of such low intensity that they do not draw attention to themselves, or the state of having ceased to produce sounds; this latter sense can be extended to apply to the…
A plant that was used in classical antiquity as a seasoning and as a medicine. Legend said that this plant was a gift from the god Apollo.
Magical silver apples can be found on Emhain Abhlach, the Isle of Apple Trees.

The woodcutter returned the same answer when a silver axe was brought to the surface by Hermes. Only when his own axe is found does he claim it. Impressed by his honesty, Hermes allows him to keep all three axes.
A tree that represents entry into the Celtic Otherworld. It is also associated with Manannán mac Lir, an Irish sea deity with strong affiliation to Tír na nÓg.
In folklore, a silver bullet is often one of the few weapons that are effective against a werewolf, vampire, witch, or other supernatural being.

In Norse mythology, Singasteinn (Old Norse "singing stone" or "chanting stone") is an object that appears in the account of Loki and Heimdall's fight in the form of seals. The object is solely attested in the skaldic poem Húsdrápa.
A sword that would sing in battle.
One of the most sacred musical instruments in ancient Egypt, which was believed to hold powerful magical properties. It was also shaken to avert the flooding of the Nile and to frighten away Set.
(Magic Tablecloth), a magic tablecloth is spread on the ground, saying the magic words and food and drink aplenty will appear.
Skin is the layer of usually soft, flexible outer tissue covering the body of a vertebrate animal, with three main functions: protection, regulation, and sensation.

Skofnung (Old Norse: Skǫfnungr) is in medieval Icelandic literature the sword of legendary Danish king Hrólf Kraki. According to Hrólfs saga kraka, it was "the best of all swords that have been carried in northern lands."
A stone that can heal wounds made by the sword Skofnung.
Skull symbolism is the attachment of symbolic meaning to the human skull. The most common symbolic use of the skull is as a representation of death.

The sky is an unobstructed view upward from the surface of the Earth. It includes the atmosphere and outer space. It may also be considered a place between the ground and outer space, thus distinct from outer space.
Skíðblaðnir (Old Norse: [ˈskiːðˌblɑðnez̠], 'assembled from thin pieces of wood'), sometimes anglicized as Skidbladnir or Skithblathnir, is the best of ships in Norse mythology.
A sacred stone venerated in Slavic and Finnic pagan practices.
A potion is a liquid that contains "medicine, poison, or something that is supposed to have magic powers." It derives from the Latin word potio which refers to a drink or the act of drinking.
Was used by Lugh to slay his grandfather, Balor the Strong-Smiter in the Cath Maige Tuired according to the brief accounts in the Lebor Gabála Érenn.
The mirror used by the god Tezcatlipoca to see the whole cosmos.

A snail is a shelled gastropod. The name is most often applied to land snails, terrestrial pulmonate gastropod molluscs. However, the common name snail is also used for most of the members of the molluscan class Gastropoda that have a…

Snakes are limbless reptiles of the squamate suborder Serpentes. Closely related to lizards and the tuatara, snakes are ectothermic, amniote, air-breathing vertebrates with an elongated rope-like body covered by overlapping scales, and…

An adder stone is a type of stone, usually glassy, with a naturally occurring hole through it. Such stones, which usually consist of flint, have been discovered by archaeologists in both Britain and Egypt.

Snow is a form of solid atmospheric precipitation consisting of individual ice crystals that grow while suspended in the air—usually within clouds—and then fall, accumulating on the ground, where they undergo further changes.
A talking mirror that serves Snow White's stepmother by answering her questions.
Sobek caught the Four sons of Horus in a net in the Nile river.
Depicted riding a quadriga on the reverse of a Roman coin.

A substance that had the power to cut through or disintegrate stone, iron and diamond. King Solomon is said to have used it in the building of the First Temple in Jerusalem in the place of cutting tools.
Soma (Sanskrit: सोम, romanized: soma) is a ritual drink of importance in the Historical Vedic religion of the early Vedic Indo-Aryans. The Rigveda mentions it, particularly in the Soma Mandala.
Soria Moria Castle (Norwegian: Soria Moria slott) is a Norwegian fairy tale made famous by Peter Christen Asbjørnsen and Jørgen Moe in their classical Norske Folkeeventyr.
The smallest flash of fire can signify a beginning of awareness or creative power still waiting to grow.
Created by Hephaestus and given to Peleus at his wedding with Thetis.
The Spear of Fuchai (Chinese: 吳王夫差矛; pinyin: Wú wáng fūchà máo) is the spear of King Fuchai of Wu, the archrival of King Goujian of Yue. It was unearthed in Jiangling, Hubei in November 1983.
See Lances: Bleeding Lance and Holy Lance (below).

Lugh or Lug (Old Irish: [l̪uɣ]; modern Irish: Lú [l̪ˠuː]) is a figure in Irish mythology. A member of the Tuatha Dé Danann, a group of supernatural beings, Lugh is portrayed as a warrior, a king, a master craftsman and a saviour.

A sphere (from Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra) 'ball') is a surface analogous to the circle, a curve. In solid geometry, a sphere is the set of points that are all at the same distance r from a given point in three-dimensional space.
A sphinx ( SFINKS; Ancient Greek: σφίγξ, pronounced [spʰíŋks]; pl. sphinxes or sphinges ) is a mythical creature with the head of a human, the body of a lion, and the wings of an eagle.
Spiders (order Araneae) are air-breathing arthropods that have eight limbs, chelicerae with fangs generally able to inject venom, and spinnerets that extrude silk.
A spindle is a straight spike, usually made from wood, used for spinning, twisting fibers such as wool, flax, hemp, and cotton into yarn.
The body's sustaining column becomes an axis connecting height and depth, uprightness and the support of life.

In mathematics, a spiral is a curve which emanates from a point, moving further away as it revolves around the point. It is a subtype of whorled patterns, a broad group that also includes concentric objects.
The Sri Yantra, Shri Yantra, or Shri Chakra (Sanskrit: श्री यन्त्र, IAST: śrī yantra) is the geometric form of Divine Mother used in the Shri Vidya school of Hinduism.
The Shrivatsa (Sanskrit: श्रीवत्स; IAST: Śrīvatsa, lit. 'Beloved of Śrī') is an ancient symbol, considered auspicious in Hinduism and other Indian religious traditions.
The St. Louis Light, St. Louis Ghost Light, or St. Louis Ghost Train is a supposed paranormal phenomenon seen near St. Louis, Saskatchewan, Canada.
The Staff of Moses, also known as the Rod of Moses or Staff of God, is mentioned in the Bible and Quran as a walking stick used by Moses.

A staircase or stairway is a flight or series of flights of stairs. It is used to connect walkways between floors so that one can move in height. A stairwell is a shaft in a building where a staircase is located.
A cosmic column which joins the heaven (Svarga) and the earth (prithvi).

The six-pointed star made of two interlaced triangles, called in Hebrew Magen David, the "Shield of David". Today the most recognised symbol of Judaism and of the Jewish people, it stands at the centre of the flag of Israel.
A symbol of the ancient Sumerian goddess Inanna and her East Semitic counterpart Ishtar. Because Ishtar was associated with the planet Venus, the star is also known as the Star of Venus.

In geology, a rock (also called a stone) is any naturally occurring solid mass or aggregate of minerals or mineraloid matter. It is categorized by the minerals included, its chemical composition, and the way in which it is formed.

entries.t: Stone and Ring of Eluned the Fortunate
entries.o: A cloak of invisibility owned by Merlin.
A stone described in Diu Crône. Sir Gawain wins from the knight Fimbeus and it offers him protection against the fiery breath of dragons and the magic of the sorcerer Laamorz.

The Stone of Scone (; Scottish Gaelic: An Lia Fàil, meaning Stone of Destiny, also called clach-na-cinneamhuinn; Scots: Stane o Scone) is an oblong block of red sandstone that was used in the coronation of Scottish monarchs until the 13th…
A precious or enduring material form can stand for concentrated value and psychic totality in particular symbolic contexts.

A storm is any disturbed state of the natural environment or the atmosphere of an astronomical body. It may be marked by significant disruptions to normal conditions such as strong wind, tornadoes, hail, thunder and lightning (a…

A stranger is a person who is unknown or unfamiliar to another person or group. Because of this unknown status or unfamiliarity, a stranger may be perceived as a threat until their identity and character can be ascertained.
The novice’s ambiguous placement outside ordinary categories is likened to being socially unseen—neither the prior role nor the successor role.

In Buddhism, a stupa (Sanskrit: स्तूप, lit. 'heap', IAST: stūpa; Pali: thūpa) is a domed hemispherical structure containing several types of sacred relics, including images, statues, metals, and śarīra—the remains of Buddhist monks or…
Experiences that escaped deliberate notice may remain psychologically active and return indirectly, sometimes in dreams.
In Henry’s dream, salvaged locomotives can suggest previously inaccessible energy or initiative becoming available again.
A bloodstained piece of cloth that is claimed to be the cloth wrapped around the head of Jesus Christ after he died.

In Hindu mythology, the Sudarshana Chakra (Sanskrit: सुदर्शनचक्र) is a divine spinning disc, attributed to Vishnu. The Sudarshana Chakra is generally portrayed on the right rear hand of the four hands of Vishnu, who also holds the…
The earliest understanding of the Sun was that of a disk in the sky, whose presence above the horizon creates day and whose absence causes night.

A sun cross, solar cross, or wheel cross is a solar symbol consisting of an equilateral cross inside a circle. The design is frequently found in the symbolism of prehistoric cultures, particularly during the Neolithic to Bronze Age periods…
The Woman of the Apocalypse is clothed with the sun.
A magical headband which, once put on, can never be removed. With a special chant, the band will tighten and cause unbearable pain.

entries.t: Sun, Moon and Stars in Myth
entries.o: Stories about celestial bodies translate their motions and visible qualities into accounts of divine kinship, order and conflict.
Sunset (or sundown) is the disappearance of the Sun at the end of the Sun path, below the horizon of the Earth (or any other astronomical object in the Solar System) due to its rotation.
Support comes through a protective figure, gift or sign once the protagonist is involved in the adventure.
(Surtr's fire), the fire with which the giant Surtr will burn the world with fire, thus destroying it.
Drawn by seven horses.

Svalinn is a legendary shield in Nordic mythology which stands in front of Sun, protecting the world from her heat. It has been suggested to be part of a continuous tradition of solar imagery dating back to the Nordic Bronze Age.
(Sleep Thorn), used to put an adversary into a deep sleep from which they would not awaken for a long time.
Adils' prized ring in the Hrólfr Kraki's saga.

Swans are birds of the genus Cygnus within the family Anatidae. The swans' closest relatives include geese and ducks. Swans are grouped with the closely related geese in the subfamily Anserinae, forming the tribe Cygnini.
A magic robe made of swan feathers belonging to a swan maiden.

g: Various, including Buddhism, Hinduism, and Jainism
entries.o: A cross with its arms bent at right angles: one of the oldest and most widespread signs in the world. In Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism it has been a sacred symbol of good fortune and well-being for thousands of years, and it still is,…

Swimming is the self-propulsion of a person through water, usually for recreation, sport, exercise, or survival. Swimmers achieve locomotion by coordinating limb and body movements to achieve a level of buoyancy and hydrodynamic thrust…
A sword is an edged, bladed weapon intended for manual cutting or thrusting. Its blade, longer than that of a knife or dagger, is attached to a hilt and can be straight or curved.

Or Caliburn, a sword in the Arthurian legend which only the rightful king of Britain can pull from the stone; sometimes associated with Excalibur. In Mallory, the sword in the stone is not Excalibur and is not named.
The Sword of Attila, also called the Sword of Mars or Sword of God, was the legendary weapon carried by Attila the Hun.
The Sword of Damocles is an ancient Greek moral anecdote, an allusion to the imminent and ever-present peril faced by those in positions of power.

Norse mythology contains references to various named weapons wielded by specific characters. The oldest references sometimes offer nothing except a name for the weapon, but some of them include more detail on the weapon and what makes it…

A sword of justice is a ceremonial sword that is used to signify a monarch's supreme judicial power. In some cases, this may have been an executioner's sword that was no longer used for executions, becoming instead a ceremonial one.
Laban () is a figure in the First Book of Nephi, near the start of the Book of Mormon, a scripture of the Latter Day Saint movement.
A magic sword that makes its wielder victorious in the battle or the hunt.

The Sword of Saint Peter (Polish: Miecz świętego Piotra) is a religious relic held in the Poznań Archdiocesan Museum. It is claimed to be the sword with which the Apostle Peter cut off the right ear of the high priest's servant at the time…
The flaming sword of the fire giant king Surtr which he uses to slay Freyr and cover the realms in fire at the end of Ragnarök, possibly the same as Freyr's sword.
Phra Saeng Khan Chai Si or Phra Saeng Khan Chai Sri (Thai: พระแสงขรรค์ชัยศรี, the "Venerable Sword of Victory", "Great Sword of Victory") is part of the royal regalia of the King of Thailand.

One of the swords wielded by Sir Balin. After his death, Merlin sealed it in the float stone where it remained until it was drawn by Sir Galahad. After Galahad, the sword passes to Sir Lancelot who fatally wounds Sir Gawain with it.
The Syamantaka (Sanskrit: स्यमन्तक, romanized: Syamantaka) is a legendary jewel featured in Hindu literature, regarded to be blessed with magical powers. It is described to be a ruby.
A symbol is a mark, sign, or word that indicates, signifies, or is understood as representing an idea, object, relationship, or mathematical formula.
An enacted or imagined ending of an old identity that makes an altered stage of life conceivable.
For Eliade, symbols disclose connections beyond isolated practical use while leaving their physical and historical reality intact.
Darkness, enclosure or apparent destruction evokes the possibility of emerging in a changed form.
Szczerbiec (Polish pronunciation: [ˈʂt͡ʂɛr.bʲɛt͡s]) is the ceremonial sword used in the coronations of most Polish monarchs from 1320 to 1764.

In Mesopotamian mythology, the Tablet of Destinies (Sumerian: 𒁾𒉆𒋻𒊏 dub namtarra; Akkadian: ṭup šīmātu, ṭuppi šīmāti) was envisaged as a clay tablet inscribed with cuneiform writing, also impressed with cylinder seals, which, as a permanent…
In the Hebrew Bible, were the two pieces of stone inscribed with the Ten Commandments when Moses ascended Mount Sinai as written in the Book of Exodus.

According to the Hebrew Bible, the Tablets of the Law (also Tablets of Stone, Stone Tablets, or Tablets of Testimony; Biblical Hebrew: לוּחֹת הַבְּרִית lūḥōṯ habbǝrīṯ "tablets of the covenant", לֻחֹת הָאֶבֶן luḥōṯ hāʾeḇen or לֻחֹת אֶבֶן…

In Chinese philosophy, a taijitu (Chinese: 太極圖; pinyin: tàijítú; Wade–Giles: tʻai⁴chi²tʻu²) is a symbol or diagram (圖; tú) representing taiji (太極; tàijí; 'utmost extreme') in both its monist (wuji) and its dualist (yin and yang) forms.
(Treasure Ship), a mythical ship piloted through the heavens by the Seven Lucky Gods during the first three days of the New Year.

The Talaria of Mercury (Latin: tālāria) or The Winged Sandals of Hermes (Ancient Greek: πτηνοπέδῑλος, ptēnopédilos or πτερόεντα πέδιλα, pteróenta pédila) are winged sandals, a symbol of the Greek messenger god Hermes (Roman equivalent…
A form of trees in sapient mythologies and stories.
A giant bronze automaton to protect Europa in Crete from pirates and invaders.
(Arthur's Harp), the name of the constellation of Lyra in Wales.
The Tarnhelm is a magic helmet in Richard Wagner's Der Ring des Nibelungen (written 1848–1874, first performed 1876). It was crafted by Mime at the demand of his brother Alberich.
Siegfried's magical cloak that made the wearer invisible (Nibelungenlied).
The missile fired by Lugh from the Sling-stone.
A symbol of Mithraic mysteries. Origin given: 2nd century CE.
Taurus (♉︎; Ancient Greek: Ταῦρος, romanized: Taûros, Latin for "bull") is the second astrological sign in the modern zodiac. It spans from 30° to 60° of the zodiac.
Tears (tear film) are a transparent fluid secreted primarily by the lacrimal glands (tear gland) found in the eyes of all land mammals.
Which are produced when the sun god Ra cries, and become honey bees upon touching the ground.
Shiva gave Barbarika three infallible arrows (Teen Baan). A single arrow was enough to destroy all opponents in any war, and it would then return to Barbarika's quiver.
A tooth (pl.: teeth) is a hard, calcified structure found in the jaws (or mouths) of many vertebrates and used to break down food.
A temple (from the Latin templum) is a place of worship, a building used for spiritual rituals and activities such as prayer and sacrifice.
A defended opening marks the boundary between ordinary identities and a ritually altered mode of being.
In Nahuatl literally "god mushroom"—compound of the words teo(tl) (god) and nanácatl (mushroom).

A collection of terracotta sculptures depicting the armies of Qin Shi Huang, the first Emperor of China. The figures include warriors, chariots and horses whose purpose was to protect the emperor in his afterlife.
An Indo-European pattern of kingship or divinity attributes effective magical constraint to the commanding figure, alongside more juridical sovereignty.
Contemplation of interminable worldly change and rebirth can produce urgency to overcome the condition of finite existence.
A symbol of Pythagoreanism. Origin given: 6th century BCE.
An iron bed used by Procrustes in which he would place his victims inside of.
Which features in the origin story of Taliesin, who accidentally obtains the awen from it while stirring it for Cerridwen.
A symbol of Community of Christ. Origin given: 1874.

The ship built in the Epic of Gilgamesh by Utnapishtim and the craftspeople of his village at the request of Enki Ea to hold his wife and relatives, as well as the village craftspeople, the animals to be saved, and various grains and seeds.
(Silverpilen, "the Silver Arrow"), a silver colored ghost train said to roam the Stockholm Metro as part of several urban legends.

William H. Pickering announced the discovery of a tenth satellite of Saturn. The photographic plates on which it supposedly appeared, thirteen in all, spanned a period between April 17 and July 8, 1904.

13 (thirteen) is the natural number following 12 and preceding 14. Folklore surrounding the number 13 appears in many cultures around the world: one theory is that this is due to the cultures employing lunar-solar calendars (there are…

entries.t: Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
g: Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
entries.o: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain (Welsh: Tri Thlws ar Ddeg Ynys Prydain) are a series of items in late-medieval Welsh tradition. Lists of the items appear in texts dating to the 15th and 16th centuries.
Driven across the sky by Thor and pulled by his two goats Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjóstr.
A fine line holds together the fragile and the continuous, connecting stories of destiny, guidance, life, and relationship.
The magical ball of thread given to Theseus by Ariadne to help him navigate the Labyrinth.

3 (three) is a number, numeral and digit. It is the natural number following 2 and preceding 4, and is the smallest odd prime number and the only prime preceding a square number. It has religious and cultural significance in many societies.
Of Japan, consisting of the Kusanagi, the jewel necklace Yasakani no Magatama, and the mirror Yata no Kagami.
The limen between rooms or worlds marks both separation and possible reconciliation, particularly between sacred and ordinary domains.
A presence at the margin of the known world represents both the risk of crossing and the limits of an earlier horizon.

A throne is the seat of state of a potentate or dignitary, especially the seat occupied by a sovereign (or viceroy) on state occasions; or the seat occupied by a pope or bishop on ceremonial occasions.
The mythical Iranian King Jamshid saved mankind from a winter destined to kill every living creature. He constructed a throne made of precious gems.
The reigning centre of God of the Abrahamic religions: primarily Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. The throne is said by various holy books to reside beyond the Seventh Heaven.
